description:
Indian River County’s Adopt-a-Road Program provides an opportunity for local organizations and individuals to contribute to the cleanliness and appearance of our community by adopting designated roadways and participating in litter cleanup activities.
In 2024, administration of the Adopt-a-Road Program transitioned to the Natural Resources Stormwater Division from the Public Works Traffic Division. The transition allows the Stormwater Division to incorporate the program more directly into its public education, community outreach, and stormwater management efforts, while maintaining coordination with the Public Works Traffic Division.
Purpose and Benefits:
The Adopt-a-Road Program supports several community and stormwater management objectives, including:Reducing litter and debris along County roadways.
Improving the appearance and cleanliness of public roadways.
Providing opportunities for residents, organizations, and community groups to participate in environmental stewardship.
Increasing public awareness of litter prevention and its connection to stormwater quality.
Strengthening partnerships between the County and members of the community.
Supporting documentation and public education efforts associated with the County’s Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) permit.

description:
Indian River County has entered into an MOU with the State of Florida Attorney General's Office that serves as the allocation agreement between the State of Florida and the local governments on the settlement of various opioid cases. As part of the MOU, money goes into a City/County Fund, a Regional Fund, and a State Fund. Indian River County receives a portion of these monies and has an agreement with Southeast Florida Behavorial Health Network to administer and disperse the opioid monies to the organizations approved by the Board.
In addition to the state-administered opioid funds, Indian River County occasionally has an opportunity to receive direct distribution of opioid settlement monies. Recently, the County Attorney's office learned of a new national opioid settlement with Albertsons grocery/pharmacy. The Albertsons national settlement totals $774 million and it resolves claims that the grocery and pharmacy improperly dispensed prescription painkillers and failed to prevent opioid misuse. The settlement funds are being distributed to states, local governments, and tribes. In order to participate, the Board must approve the attached Subdivision Participation and Release Form. Although the amount that the County will receive is unclear, the funds will come directly to the County and will be distributed to the 19th Judicial Circuit Drug Court programs and used for assessment, treatment, testing and wrap-around services, such as housing and transportation.
title: Participation in New National Opioid Settlement with Albertsons

description:
As part of HB 1375, enacted in 2007, the Legislature revised section 420.9076, F.S., to require that local governments establish a local Affordable Housing Advisory Committee (AHAC). On March 18, 2008, the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners (BCC) approved Resolution 2008-038 to establish Indian River County’s AHAC. According to state law, the principal responsibility of the AHAC is to submit a report to the local governing body that includes a recommendation on, or evaluation of the affordable housing incentives identified in Paragraphs A through K of Section 420.9076 (4), F.S. (see page 2 of this staff report).
Consistent with the provisions of Section 420.9076 F.S. (up until the 2020 legislative session), every three years, the AHAC was required to review the local government’s established policies and procedures, ordinances, land development regulations, and comprehensive plans and recommend specific actions or initiatives to encourage or facilitate affordable housing, while protecting the ability of a property to appreciate in value. Pursuant to House Bill 1339, adopted during the 2020 Florida Legislative Session, the triennial requirement changed to an annual requirement starting in 2021.
The County’s first AHAC report was approved by the BCC on December 9, 2008, submitted to the Florida Housing Finance Corporation (FHFC) before its December 31, 2008, due date, and thereafter approved by the FHFC. Subsequent AHAC reports were prepared, recommended for approval by AHAC, approved by the BCC, and submitted to the FHFC in 2011, 2014, 2017, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. The County’s next AHAC report is due to the state by December 31, 2026. To meet that deadline, staff have prepared the 2026 incentives review and recommendations report for AHAC’s consideration.
title: Review of the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee 2025 Incentives Review and Recommendation Report

description:
The subject properties, comprising approximately ±1.82 acres, are located on the west side of Enterprise Road, south of State Road 60. The properties are zoned CG, General Commercial (Attachment 1) with a Future Land Use designation of C/I (Commercial/Industrial) (Attachment 2). The property is situated within the established S.R.60 & I-95, commercial and industrial node [Comprehensive Plan: Table 2.5, Commercial/industrial Nodes (2006)]. The properties are located within the SR 60 Corridor Overlay, which contains provisions that promote the design of attractive buildings and complementary landscaping, as set forth in Section 911.19 of Indian River County’s Land Development Regulations (LDRs).
The applicant’s justification letter states, “The subject property is currently vacant and carries a Future Land Use designation of Commercial/Industrial (C/I); no change to the Future Land Use Map is requested. The rezoning is intended to bring the two lots into conformance with the industrial character and IL zoning pattern already established throughout the balance of Vero West Business Park.”
The subject properties are currently undeveloped. The proposed rezoning from CG to IL would extend the established IL zoning pattern within Vero West Business Park and allow the parcels to be reviewed and developed under consistent industrial zoning standards. The request is compatible with the existing C/I Future Land Use designation and supports a logical and cohesive development pattern within the SR 60 and I-95 commercial/industrial node and the SR 60 Corridor.
Existing Land Use Pattern
The surrounding area is largely undeveloped; therefore, the existing land use pattern is best understood through the area’s zoning history and current zoning configuration described below. The subject properties have been zoned CG since the original 1975–1985 Indian River County Zoning Atlas, which placed commercial zoning along the SR 60 frontage. Most of the surrounding commercial and industrial properties fall within Vero West Business Park, which was re-platted in 2025. The park was platted around the pre-existing CG and IL zoning boundaries, retaining the existing zoning configuration within the subdivision.
To the north, properties remain largely undeveloped and are zoned CG, extending toward the SR 60 frontage. To the east, across Enterprise Road, properties are also zoned CG and generally undeveloped. To the south, adjoining properties are zoned IL, Light Industrial, and extend into the larger industrial portion of Vero West Business Park. To the west, adjoining CG-zoned land contains a lake that accommodates drainage and provides approximately 300 feet of separation between the industrially zoned portion of the park and an established residential community along 100th Avenue, known as Kenilworth Estates, The residential community is zoned A-1, Agricultural District, and was platted in 1960.
Since the subject properties remain vacant, the proposed rezoning from CG to IL would extend the adjoining industrial zoning district before development occurs. The request would support more cohesive site planning within Vero West Business Park and remain compatible with the existing C/I Future Land Use designation.
Zoning District Differences
There are similarities and differences between the uses permitted within the CG and IL zoning districts (Attachment 3). The distinctions between these two zoning districts are best illustrated through their respective purpose statements. These purpose statements provide a clear framework for understanding the intent and scope of each district's allowable uses and development potential. The purpose statements are as follows:
CG: General Commercial District: The CG, General Commercial district, is intended to provide areas for the development of general retail sales and selected service activities. The CG district is not intended to provide for heavy commercial activities, such as commercial service uses, heavy repair services or industrial uses. The commercial districts are established to implement the Indian River County Comprehensive Plan policies for commercial development. These districts are intended to permit the development of commercial property to provide an efficient use of land and public infrastructure, promote the economic well-being of the county, protect the natural resources and beauty of the county, and ensure commercial development is compatible with existing and proposed development.
IL: Light Industrial District: The IL, Light Industrial district, is intended to provide opportunities for limited manufacturing and industrial uses and to promote the establishment of employment centers which are accessible to urban services and facilities, the area labor force, and local industrial and business markets while minimizing the potential for any adverse impacts upon nearby properties. The Industrial districts are established to implement the Indian River County Comprehensive Plan policies for Industrial development. These districts are intended to permit the development of industrial property to provide an efficient use of land and public infrastructure, promote the economic well-being of the county and ensure industrial development is compatible with existing and proposed development.
title: Vero West Business Park Rezoning

description:
The owner of the property (hereinafter “developer”) located at 3601 Indian River Boulevard located north of the Vero Beach Country Club, west of Indian River Boulevard, south of 37th Street and east of the 407 building has requested an access easement across a County-owned parcel located at 3100 Par Drive. This County-owned parcel was obtained as an uneconomic remainder of a taking for development of Indian River Boulevard. The developer’s property also is the remainder of a parcel that was taken by the County for Indian River Boulevard. In the taking of the developer’s property (Parcel 109) the court entered an order requiring the county to allow the developer to gain access to its parcel/development from Indian River Boulevard. (see the attached court order for reference). This proposed Access Agreement is to ensure the County's compliance with the court order.
The developer would be allowed to have access from Indian River Boulevard via right turn in, left turn in, and right turn out movements. The Developer will also construct a U-turn south of the entrance in order to allow the right turn-out to perform a U-turn and continue north on Indian River Boulevard.
This particular project is located in the City of Vero Beach and has received site plan approval by the City. The traffic and access to the road is through the County as Indian River Boulevard is a County-owned road. The proposed location for the Access Easement is in accordance with the approved city of Vero Beach site plan.
The construction of Access Easement, along with all other requirements for the construction of the same, will be performed by the developer. The Access Easement Agreement calls for all maintenance and costs thereof to be borne by the Developer. There is also a requirement for the developer to obtain liability insurance coverage listing the County as an additional insured as well as indemnification and hold harmless clauses.
The agreement will allow for the County to comply with the prior court order dated May 14, 1992, and avoid any potential litigation over said court order.
title: Access Easement Agreement - ELORA Project

description:
Lot 5, Plat of Indian River Mall is an undeveloped 4.7-acre parcel of property on State Road 60, just west of the Wendy’s restaurant near the main entrance to the Indian River Mall. It is owned by IR Mall Associates, LTD and marketed by REDEVGROUP, Inc. At the time the plat for the Mall was moving forward, environmental studies revealed the existence of hand fern, a species of critical concern, on the mature trees growing on Lot 5. In 1994, as a condition of County Resolution 94-93, which serves as the Development Order (D.O.) for the Indian River Mall, a conservation easement was established over Lot 5. The Lot 5 conservation easement contained a clause which allowed release of the easement provided alternative conservation land of equal or greater environmental value was protected to fulfill the intent of the D.O.
Early in 2018, REDEVGROUP approached the County with a report concluding that the hand fern was no longer found on Lot 5. REDEVGROUP asked the Board to release the conservation over Lot 5 in exchange for two parcels:
• Property 1: “The Alice Siew Property,” approximately 9.17 acres (4 contiguous tax parcels) of riverfront coastal wetlands north of and adjacent to the County-owned Oyster Bar Marsh Conservation Area; or
• Property 2: “The Kinner Property,” approximately 10.3 acres of riverfront coastal wetlands south of Quay Dock Road, north of Spoonbill Marsh, adjacent to conservation land owned by the Indian River Land Trust (IRLT). Also included was a payment of $291,819.00 to the County to be used for public access improvements to county-owned conservation lands.
At its meeting on June 12, 2018, the Board of County Commissioners approved an Agreement between Indian River County and REDEVGROUP, Inc. to allow for release of the conservation easement on Indian River Mall Lot 5 in exchange for alternative conservation land and special development restrictions on Lot 5. The development restrictions included the following:
• The combined pervious and storm water areas of the Lot must not be less than 44% of the total property area, with no building, paving or construction on the southernmost 75’ of the Lot. (that area to be used for landscaping, water retention and signage). • At least 6 specimen trees preserved on site.
• State Road 60 corridor code requirement would apply.
• No single building footprint could exceed 7,200 square feet with all buildings being separated by at least 50 feet.
Three months after the June 12 agreement was approved, REDEVGROUP approached staff with a First Addendum to Amend Agreement that contained a third alternative proposal that the Board considered at its September 11, 2018 meeting. The third alternative was a combination of portions of both the Siew Property and the Kinner Property. This third proposed alternative was described as follows:
• REVDEVGROUP conveyance of the +10.3 acre Kinner Property to the IRLT (Indian River Land Trust) with a conservation easement over +8.8 acres in favor of Indian River County covering all but the east 150 feet of the Kinner Property, together with conveyance of +7.87 acres of the Siew Property to the County (all but the eastern +1.3 acres of the originally proposed Siew Property).
The third alternative exchange option, which combined and protected the majority of both the Siew and Kinner properties (i.e., +16.67 protected acres combined), provided greater ecological value than the current 4.7 acre I. R. Mall Lot 5 easement, and therefore was approved by the Board on September 11, 2018.
An aerial photo of Lot 5 is depicted in Figure 1 below.
Figure 1. Aerial Photo of Lot 5, Plat of Indian River Mall
Staff was again approached by REDEVGROUP for a Third Addendum to the original Agreement. As part of the original Agreement, four deed restrictions were recorded concerning Lot 5. REDEVGROUP asked to amend the deed restrictions concerning the 7,200 square foot limitation to allow the size of one building to be 7,800 square feet, asserting that one of the potential restaurants interested in building on Lot 5 has a standard template which is just less than 7,800 square feet. In exchange for the size increase for the one building, the remaining buildings could not exceed an average of 7,200 square feet. On November 10, 2020, the Board approved the amendment, but increased the building size limit to Staff to 8,000 square feet with no change in the other restrictions.
On July 6, 2021, REDEVGROUP appeared before the BCC with a proposed Fourth Addendum to Agreement as Texas Roadhouse, Inc. had expressed interest in building a restaurant on Lot 5. With the advent of COVID 19, restaurant designs changed, including increased room for carryout service, increased room when waiting for a table, greater distances between tables and additional outdoor dining space. REDEVGROUP asked to amend the 8,000 square foot building restriction and increase it to 8,225 square feet in size. The Board approved the expansion to 8,225 square feet as there were no other changes to the original restrictions on Lot 5 tree preservation, building sizes or open space requirements.
On November 8, 2022, REDEVGROUP appeared before the BCC with a proposed Fifth Addendum to Agreement as Texas Roadhouse, Inc. required a larger footprint that would exceed the 8,225 square foot footprint previously approved. REDEVGROUP asked the Board to allow Roadhouse to increase the building footprint of the restaurant to 9,400 square feet. The larger footprint was to account for increased sizes for carryout service, waiting area for a table, distances between tables and covered outdoor/open air dining space. As with the earlier addendums, there were no change to the original restrictions on Lot 5 tree preservation, other building sizes or open space requirements.
REDEVGROUP now asks the Board to allow an increase the building footprint of the restaurant to 12,000 square feet. As with the earlier addendums, there is no change to the original restrictions on Lot 5 tree preservation, other building sizes or open space requirements.
title: Redevgroup Inc. Request for 6th Addendum

description:
Floravon Shores is a community that is adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon (IRL). Indian River County Department of Utility Services (IRCDUS) completed Floravon Shores Phase 1 Septic-to-Sewer (S2S) project on 110th Place in 2005. Floravon Shores Phase 2 S2S will extend sewer service to nineteen (19) properties on 110th Street that are served by onsite treatment and disposal systems (OSTDS). These septic systems potentially leach harmful nutrients into groundwater that leads to the IRL.
On June 8, 2021, the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners (BCC), approved Work Order No.2 (WO 2) to Schulke, Bittle & Stoddard, LLC (SBS), under its continuing contract agreement with the county dated April 17, 2018, in the amount of $44,750.00. Under WO 2, SBS provides professional engineering and technical services for design, permitting, administrative, bidding, and construction services. The BCC approved Amendment 1 to WO 2 on December 9, 2025, in the amount of $29,730.00 to provide additional administrative, bidding, and construction services. With Amendment 1 the total approved budget for WO 2 increased to $74,480.00.
Recommendation of bid award to Treasure Coast Infrastructure (TCI) of Stuart was originally planned for the January 27, 2026 BCC agenda. However, the award was removed from the agenda after publication to defer until after a community meeting was held with the residents of Floravon Shores. The Procurement Manager contacted TCI and inquired if they would consider honoring their bid to allow more time for the community meeting to be held, to which TCI agreed. On April 7, 2026, the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners (BCC) awarded Bid No. 2025045 for the Floravon Shores S2S project to TCI.
Because the award was made approximately six months after the bid opening (twice the time they were required to honor their bid), TCI requested an increase in the total award amount of $250,000 to cover material and subcontractor price increases, and impact to equipment availability. The Procurement Division responded to TCI’s request, stating the County is willing to consider their request based upon TCI providing the quotes used to develop their original bid and the current quotes, to substantiate the requested change. TCI was unresponsive to the County’s request and due to the length of time that had passed since bids were received, staff considered it appropriate to terminate the award to TCI and rebid the project.
title: Amendment 3 to Work Order 2 for Schulke, Bittle & Stoddard, LLC, for Floravon Shores Septic to Sewer, IRCDUS Project ID 21.19.556

description:
Each year, Indian River County receives public transportation operating assistance through the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Public Transportation Block Grant program. The FDOT Block Grant funds are combined with local funds as a match towards federal transit operating assistance received under 49 USC Ch. 53, Section 5307 (also known as the Urbanized Area Formula Grant program) and Section 5311 (also known as the Rural Area Formula Grant program). The FDOT Block Grant provides operating assistance for the County’s public transportation system, which consists of GoLine (fixed route) and Community Coach (demand response) transit services operated by the Senior Resource Association (SRA) under contract with the county.
For FY 2026/27, $801,016 has been allocated through the state Block Grant program to the county. Because the Block Grant has a 50% match requirement, the county is required to provide a local match of $801,016. As was the case in previous years, matching funds will come from the County’s normal transit allocation. Together, the Block Grant funds and local funds ($1,602,032) will be applied as a local/state match towards federal operating assistance through the Section 5307 program.
title: Approval of a Public Transportation Grant Agreement (PTGA) with the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) for a Public Transportation Block Grant

description: On April 5, 2022, the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners approved the original ARFF Agreement with the City of Vero Beach. This Agreement sets the terms and provides for Indian River County Emergency Services to provide specialty emergency response at the Vero Beach Airport. The City is responsible for the costs associated with this coverage, which they pass on to the air carriers. Due to the increasing popularity and number of daily flights, the FAA requires the classification of the airport to increase to Index C. This requires more intensive capabilities and staffing for ARFF response. Based upon this need, Indian River County Emergency Services has negotiated this Amended and Restated ARFF Agreement to provide greater cost-sharing for training, expenses, and expanded staffing capabilities. The amendment also clarifies the parties’ responsibilities relating to equipment and maintenance. The term of the Agreement remains the same. The updated payments begin once staff is actively in place to provide the updated services. The City of Vero Beach approved the Amendment on October 14, 2026.

The proposed LDR amendments being presented for the BCC’s consideration involve changes to the Professional Office (PRO) zoning district. The PRO district is intended to provide for low-intensity office and commercial development in areas that may serve as a transition between residential areas and more intensive commercial uses. The PRO district is currently underutilized within the unincorporated County, with only nine properties totaling approximately 14.85 acres presently zoned PRO.
Staff proposes amendments to Chapters 911 and 971 intended to provide additional opportunities for low-intensity, neighborhood-serving commercial uses within the PRO district, encourage commercial-residential mixed-use development, and revise certain development standards applicable to PRO properties.
The amendments are proposed as a single ordinance. The Board of County Commissioners is to consider the proposed LDR amendments and make a motion to adopt, adopt with modifications, or deny the proposed ordinance.

description:
Indian River County Department of Utilities Services (IRCDUS) owns and operates a consolidated water system that provides potable water throughout Indian River County. IRCDUS utilizes groundwater from the Upper Floridan Aquifer (UFA) treated with Nanofiltration (NF) and raw water bypass blending. Allocation for IRCDUS is provided by St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD) under Consumptive Use Permit (CUP) Number 10524-11, which limits flows to 16.228 MGD and this permit expires in October 2031. Projections performed by IRCDUS under the Integrated Water Master Plan (IWMP) indicate that the average daily raw water use will exceed the allocated capacity in 2031. The raw water flow needed to support the projected potable flow demands is expected to exceed the current permitted allocation prior to the CUP expiration date. As such, IRCDUS needs to secure additional allocation via SJRWMD and construct and place online additional UFA well sites prior to 2031.
IRCDUS currently has a deficit in raw water supply wells that limit water production capacities. As part of the CUP process, an evaluation of Hobart is required to determine the maximum treatment capacity under current conditions, which will be completed through a Capacity Analysis Report (CAR) and onsite performance testing. Any limiting factors in achieving the desired capacity will be outlined, and minor capital improvements will be identified where appropriate. This work will determine the current maximum treatment capacity of Hobart and, in doing so, identify the number of wells needed to support production firm capacity requirements.
In summary, raw water capacity, and/or, CUP limits IRC’s water production facilities’ ability to meet projected drinking water demand and must be addressed. In conjunction with the SJRWMD to secure the CUP allocation, the additional well sites will maximize the use of existing treatment infrastructure and provide additional source water for expected growth in demand. To address this shortfall, a comprehensive phased program must be implemented, proposed as follows:
Phase 1: Planning and Water Use Permitting
Phase 2A: Test Well Design, Permitting, Construction and Performance Testing
Phase 2B: Production Well Design, Permitting and Construction
Phase 2C: Design, Permitting and Construction of raw water main infrastructure
title: Approval of Work Order No.35 to Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. for Water Resources Wellfield Expansion Planning & Permitting, IRCDUS Project ID: 11.26.526.01

description:
On October 20th, The ELAP committee was approached by Raymond Darling concerning tracts of land along Route 60 near Blue Cypress Lake, mostly consisting of property within Pressley Ranch.
Mr. Darling presented to ELAP that there is a pending sale of more than 800 acres of this land to FPL for a solar farm, and he has been able to obtain the right of first refusal for a large portion of the intended purchase.
Mr. Darling already owns around 300 acres to the North and is interested in preserving the land and has asked ELAP and the BOCC to consider assisting the transaction through a conservation easement, preserving the land from development. Portions of each of the proposed parcels were previously ranked by ELAP as Tier 1, high value properties and the panel was interested in attempting to save this land for the future.
Time is of the essence as there are contracts pending with strict timelines. Pursuant to ELAP policies enacted by this Board, we can move a property forward as an emergency under situations like these.
I propose that we allow Mr. Darling to make his presentation to the Board and then approve the properties under the emergency rule. Additionally, I propose that we direct staff to begin all the necessary due diligence, including appraisals, studies, and negotiations on terms of an easement on an expedited basis. Once this necessary work is completed, the matter will be brought back to the Board for further consideration.
title: ELAP Potential Emergency Acquisition

Indian River County (The County) and our municipalities host numerous street festivals, parades, and other community events. These public gatherings can attract large crowds, which is a target for hostile action-based mass casualty incidents.
The Meridian Archer Trailer Kit 1000 is a protection system which reduces an assailant’s capability to weaponize a vehicle in targeted pedestrian areas. The kit’s included equipment list is attached to this Agenda Item for review.
The Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM) has offered a Meridian Archer Trailer Kit 1000 to the County through a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA). The MOA allows the County to have custody of the protective equipment. The County (and local law enforcement Agencies) may deploy the equipment at our discretion to increase community safety. FDEM may still access the kit by issuing a reasonable notice or during a state of emergency. The County shall be responsible for the equipment’s maintenance and upkeep while the MOA is in effect.
title: Approval of the Florida Division of Emergency Management’s Memorandum of Agreement for a Meridian Archer Trailer Kit 1000

description:
Indian River County (The County) is located on Florida’s East Coast, which is adjacent to the Atlantic Ocean. This makes the County vulnerable to hurricane impacts and other natural disasters/hazards. Restoration of electrical services is a critical component of community recovery. Florida Power and Light (FPL) is a major supplier of electrical utility services in Florida. FPL plays a critical role in the coordination of electrical power restoration in an all-hazards environment. As such, there are times when FPL needs to strategically stage power restoration equipment when a hurricane or other disaster threatens Florida’s communities.
FPL has presented a Staging Area Agreement to position power restoration equipment at the Fran Adams Soccer Field, which is located at 9450 Fellsmere Road in Sebastian, Florida. The soccer field is adjacent to the North County Aquatic Center and softball fields. FPL’s Staging Area Agreement notes that their company shall be responsible for securing the area against theft, vandalism, and site abuse. FPL shall have access to the area for as long as reasonably necessary to reinstall electrical services. FPL shall return the staging area to its previous condition when demobilization occurs.
title: Approval of Florida Power and Light Equipment Staging Area Agreement at the North County Regional Park - Fran Adams Soccer Field

description:
Adopted in 2008, the MPO’s North Indian River County Greenways Plan proposes a network of greenways in the area around Sebastian and Fellsmere. One of the proposed greenways is along the South Prong of the St. Sebastian River from CR 512 to CR 510. At its north end, the proposed greenway could connect to the Trans-Florida Central Railroad Trail, which is proposed for extension eastward as a shared use path to the Sebastian riverfront area. To the south, the St. Sebastian River Greenway has the potential to connect to a future shared use path along the 82nd Avenue corridor.
Last year, the Indian River Land Trust (IRLT) began preparation of a master plan for the St. Sebastian River Greenway, in coordination with County and City of Sebastian staff. As part of that planning effort, IRLT has also proposed that LJA Engineering, Inc. (formerly Carter Associates, Inc.) conduct a feasibility study of the first phase of the proposed greenway (from CR 512 south to an IRLT-owned parcel just south of Gladiola Avenue in Sebastian). On June 2, 2026, the Board approved for the County to contribute $6,615 towards the $22,050 cost of the feasibility study. The County share is based on the amount of linear footage of the proposed greenway owned by the County (approximately 30%).
title: Memorandum of Understanding Regarding the St. Sebastian River Greenway

description:
This is the second of two public hearings required by Florida Statute Section 163.3225 for the approval of an amendment to the Emerson Oaks Developer's Agreement. The first public hearing was held on October 6, 2026.
Emerson Oaks is a proposed residential planned development consisting of 171 Single Family lots to be located at the southwest corner of 43rd Avenue SW and 13th Street SW. This project is proposed to be constructed in 3 phases. Phase 1A consists of the model home row (seven lots), the project entrance on 13th Street SW, and the adjacent stormwater pond. Phase 1B will include 70 lots, the amenity center, and infrastructure commensurate with this phase. Phase 2 will include 94 lots (the remainder of the residential development), the project entrance on 17th Street SW, and the necessary utilities needed to support the phase 2 homes.
The original developer's agreement for this development was approved by the Board of County Commissioners on November 4, 2025. (Original Agreement attached hereto for reference.)
The developer was in the process of performing their duties under the original developer's agreement when they were approached by the Public Works Department with a request to add additional items that would otherwise be the County's responsibility — primarily the widening and paving of roads near the development.
County projects, particularly roadway projects, can be more costly because the county is required to go out to bid for project engineering and construction, along with mobilization and other associated costs for the improvements. By having the developer who is already mobilized in the area and working on their own portion of the project take over and do the county's portion, the county will save money because the developer can negotiate for cheaper prices and reduce mobilization costs. By doing the work on behalf of the county, the developer benefits by having all the areas near their developments being updated and ready to sell without having to sell homes during the county's construction period. This also benefits the public in that there will only be one construction period in that area instead of two separate construction periods in that area. This amendment to the original developer's agreement was staff initiated to attempt to obtain those benefits on behalf of the county and its current and future residents.
The cost estimate and scope of work that are to be completed by the developer are attached to the amended developer's agreement as Exhibits "E" and "F." They have been approved by the county engineering division and are what the reimbursement to the developer is based on.
The change for the scope of work and reimbursement, along with the change in date of the agreement are the sole changes to the original developer's agreement.
title: Second Public Hearing for Amended and Restated Developers Agreement Between Pulte Home Company, LLC and Indian River County - Emerson Oaks PD

description:
Currently, Indian River County Code, Chapter 104 Human Resources, Section 104.2 references the County’s Administrative Policy Manual which is maintained by the Director of Human Resources under the direction of the County Administrator. This manual includes policies, practices, and procedures that apply to managers, supervisors and employees of Indian River County.
In place of the employment-related policies reflected in the Administrative Policy Manual, Human Resources has developed an Employee Handbook. Therefore, Chapter 104, Section 104.2 Administrative Policy Manual is being amended to delete the reference to the Administrative Policy Manual and replace it with reference to an Employee Handbook as noted below.
Section 104.02. – Administrative policy manual Employee Handbook.
The director or manager of human resources shall maintain under the direction of the county administrator a policy manual an employee handbook which shall be a compilation of policies, practices, and procedures that apply to managers, supervisors and employees of Indian River County. This manual handbook shall be updated, from time to time, with the approval of the county commission. This manual employee handbook is available in electronic format in the office of director or manager of human resources, the office of each department or division, and on the county's website. All employees should be encouraged to become familiar with the contents of this manual are responsible for being familiar with the policies reflected in the employee handbook. Acknowledgement of the employee handbook will be incorporated into the employee onboarding process.
title: Public Hearing for Ordinance Amending Indian River County Code Chapter 104

description:
On January 2, 2019, the County entered into the Amended and Restated Facility Lease Agreement with Major League Baseball (MLB) doing business as Verotown, LLC (Verotown) to operate the Jackie Robinson Training Complex at the facility previously known as Historic Dodgertown. The Agreement was subsequently amended by the First Amendment executed on February 16, 2021, the Second Amendment executed on July 12, 2022, and Third Amendment executed on April 9, 2024 (Collectively “The Agreement”).
The initial term of the Agreement is ten years and eight months with three successive renewal options of five years each. The Agreement represents a partnership where the County and MLB share in the cost of facility improvements. In broad summary, under the original Agreement, the County was responsible for initial repairs on items consisting mostly of roof replacements and concession stand replacements/repairs where maintenance had been deferred during the economic downturn. Verotown agreed to be responsible for making some initial facility improvements, such as the design and construction of an indoor training facility now known as the 42 Building. Additionally, Verotown has completed facility repairs such as replacing the entire Holman Stadium seating bowl. Under the Agreement, the County reimburses Verotown for 50% of these costs within the limits of the Capital Reserve Account as set forth in the lease agreement. Other than the County-funded initial improvements as amended, the County’s annual contribution is its only obligation for facility improvements and maintenance. Verotown will be responsible for all other capital improvements and maintenance for the duration of the initial term and any renewal term. Most recently, Verotown has also completed several capital improvement projects not required under the Agreement, including the state-of-the-art conference center known as the “5” Building and is currently under construction to renovate the Dining Hall and Jackie Robinson Room. Over the course of the partnership, MLB has undertaken the following have been completed that were outside the obligations of the lease agreement:Fencing around the entire perimeter of the property, as well as installation of four electronic entry gates
Exterior site lighting upgrades to modern-style LED lighting around the villas, multipurpose field, Conference Center, Building 42, and the pool area
A second artificial turf baseball field “Field Teamwork” (we were only contractually required to provide one) including new fencing and safety netting, plus rebuilding of 6-pack bullpens adjacent, including conversion to artificial turf and addition of fencing
Purchase of portable outfield fencing and temporary backstop system to be able to utilize Field Teamwork for softball
New fencing around the entirety of the original field we converted to artificial turf
New (replacement) east batting cages (stripped down to the foundation and rebuilt), rebuilt adjacent bullpen area, added new fencing
Purchase of heavy-duty flooring to be able to utilize the turf area in Building 42 for non-traditional events (food & beverage events, etc.)
Addition of baseball technology systems at Holman Stadium – Trackman, Yakkertech, Sportlight / also in the process of adding Hawkeye/Kinatrax/ABS (install anticipated to begin this Fall/Winter)
New and extended safety netting at Holman Stadium
New LED field lighting at Holman Stadium

description:
On September 17, 2019, at the request of the Community Development Department, the Board waived the requirement for bids and authorized a direct agreement with the South-Central Planning and Development Commission (“SCPDC”) for their My Government Online (“MGO”) permitting software. Implementation was considered completed in October 2022, but not all the anticipated models have been activated. The software is used mainly for building permits, as all other departments did not support moving forward with utilizing MGO for their respective permitting types, for various reasons, primarily because they did not feel MGO performed efficiently, did not have an existing developed module for their respective functions, and would not meet the needs of our external customers, therefore an alternative solution was requested.
A Task Force, led by the County Administration Ombudsman and comprised of approximately 30 members of the following departments: Utilities, I.T./GIS, Public Works (Land Development and Right of Way), Building & Facilities Services (Life Safety and Contractor Licensing), Planning and Development Services (Code Enforcement and Environmental Planning), and Emergency Services (Fire Prevention), developed a list of requirements for a new software solution. On May 30, 2025, a Request for Information (RFI) was issued for a new software product, listing the requirements and desired functionality, with suppliers asked to indicate the extent to which their product met the requirements. A total of 22 responses to the questionnaires were received. At a publicly noticed meeting held on Thursday, September 24, 2026, the task force reviewed all 22 RFI’s and eliminated 8 suppliers for not meeting minimum requirements or being suitable for the County’s needs. The remaining 14 were discussed more fully by the Working Group, twelve of which were eliminated from consideration. Two (2) suppliers were ultimately selected to move forward, Intuitive Municipal Solutions (iMS) and GovWell, and the working group was invited to watch product demonstrations that had previously been provided.
Discussions about data migration & conversion, AI capabilities, financial payment processes, cybersecurity, GIS capabilities, plan review software capabilities were held and evaluated.
Throughout the evaluation process, iMS consistently demonstrated that it understands the needs of Florida local governments. This is important because building permitting relies on the Florida Building Code, not the Southern Building Code (SBC) or International Building Code (IBC) like other states. The system offers flexibility to adapt to the County's processes without requiring the manual processes that are now occurring with MGO. Simple process improvements can be made by designated county staff administrators versus waiting for the company to make them. iMS also provides for unlimited data migration, thereby allowing the county to utilize one system instead of three and a fully integrated platform that allows all county departments, City of Vero Beach & Department of Health to work together in one system, creating a more efficient and streamlined permitting process for both staff, the development community, and our public.
title: Approval of Permitting Software Selection and Agreements

description:
On August 20, 2026, the Sheriff notified the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners that he was opting out of the County’s benefits and moving to the Florida Sheriffs Employee Benefits Trust (FSEBT). In this notice, the Sheriff stated FSEBT would contact County representatives to negotiate a contract to provide Sheriff’s Office members with continued access to the Marathon Health Center.
On September 9, 2026, staff met with FSEBT and Sheriff’s Office representatives to discuss continued access for eligible Sheriff’s Office employees and retirees who will be enrolled in the new group health insurance plan. Our consultant, Lockton Companies, provided a per eligible per month (PEPM) access fee based on actual expenses for the year. The fee for the Sheriff’s Office would be $53.80 PEPM for the fiscal year 2026/2027 plan year. The Sheriff’s Office has approximately 605 eligible employees and retirees.
At the September 15, 2026, BOCC meeting, the Board approved the Sheriff’s Office continuing to have access to the Marathon Health and Wellness Center under a walk-on agenda item presented by the County Administrator. Following this approval, the Human Resources Director and County Attorney drafted an interlocal agreement which was submitted to the Sheriff for signature. Some suggested revisions were made at the request of the Sheriff’s Office legal counsel, and the final agreement was signed by the Sheriff on October 1, 2026, and is presented to the Board for approval. The Sheriff also signed the necessary Business Associate Agreement with Marathon regarding the handling of protected health information in compliance with HIPAA regulations.
Additionally, it was identified that Section 6.1 of the Client Agreement between the Indian River County Board of County Commissions and Marathon Health needed to be modified to specify the Sheriff’s Office is a participating group, since they are no longer a member of the County’s group health plan. The amendment to the Section 6.1 of the Client Agreement is provided to the Board for approval.
While these documents were being finalized, Human Resources confirmed with Marathon that eligible Sheriff’s Office employees and retirees were authorized by the Board to continue to have access to the health and wellness center after September 30, 2026, so they did not experience a disruption in health care as a result of the Sheriff moving group health insurance to the Florida Sheriffs Employee Benefit Trust (FSEBT).
title: Sheriff Office Access to Marathon Health and Wellness Center — Approval of Interlocal Agreement and Second Amendment to Client Agreement

description:
Currently, in accordance with Indian River County Code, Chapter 104 Human Resources, Section 104.2, the Director of Human Resources maintains the County’s Administrative Policy Manual. This manual includes policies, practices, and procedures that apply to managers, supervisors and employees of Indian River County as well as other non-employment related policies. Many of the employment related policies date back to 1989 and needed to be updated to replace outdated terms and obsolete references to reflect plain language that is more easily understood and to match current legal and social standards.
To accomplish this update, Human Resources has developed an Employee Handbook that has included review by and input from Department Directors, Assistant and Deputy County Administrators, Assistant County Attorney and County Attorney, and the County Administrator. The draft Employee Handbook was also provided to the Teamsters and IAFF unions for review and comment. The final draft is presented to the Board for approval in accordance with Indian River County Code.
In concurrence with this agenda item, Human Resources, with assistance from the County Attorney’s office, has prepared a separate agenda item proposing an amendment to Indian River County Code, Chapter 104 Human Resources, Section 104.02 – Administrative Policy Manual. This amendment replaces the reference to the Administrative Policy Manual with reference to the Employee Handbook. The Employee Handbook will replace all the employment related policies in the Administrative Policy Manual.
Once both agenda items are approved, the Employee Handbook will be announced to County employees and electronic access to the handbook will be available to all County employees on the Human Resources Staff Portal in place of the Administrative Policy Manual. A written acknowledgment of the handbook, to include instructions on how to access the handbook, will be provided to every County employee for signature and placement in their personnel file.
Access to the remaining non-employment related policies of the Administrative Policy Manual will be available on the County Administration website. These policies will be maintained by County Administration.
In addition, access to Risk Management policies that are currently housed in the Administrative Policy Manual will be moved to the Risk Management website.
title: Approval of Employee Handbook

description:
Since August 2026, the County has removed three more derelict vessels from the Indian River Lagoon, after receiving authorization from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC).
Derelict vessels are defined by the State of Florida in section 823.11,F.S. as vessels left, stored or abandoned in a wrecked, junked or substantially dismantled condition upon the waters of the state, at a port without the consent of the agency or upon private property without the consent of the owner. Derelict vessels are sinking, degraded, and inoperable, creating navigation hazards, threats to wildlife, and the environment. Vessels designated derelict undergo an extensive investigative process to locate the rightful owner for removal before being submitted to the FWC's Division of Boating and Waterways to approve removal. Natural Resources staff coordinates with FWC to remove approved derelict vessels in a timely manner to reduce risks to the Indian River Lagoon and navigational hazards.

description:
In 2005, Indian River County implemented its Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) to increase the biological productivity of the County’s beaches as sea turtle nesting habitat. Public education and outreach are key components of the HCP to achieve conservation goals.
In order to increase our educational outreach, Coastal Engineering staff is proposing to seek available grant funding to develop, install, and maintain, a series of scientifically accurate, visually engaging interpretive signs at 5 County beach access points; Wabasso, Turtle Trail, Seagrape, Tracking Station, and Round Island. Each sign would measure at 36” W x 24” H and feature a fully framed panel mounted at approximately a 45-degree angle. The signs would be positioned on dune crossovers or under pavilions, with consideration given to pedestrian walkways as to not impose additional obstacles.
Florida offers many different specialty license plate options when registering a motor vehicle, with revenue from the sale of those plates directly supporting the cause represented. Proceeds from the sale of Florida’s sea turtle specialty license plate, the state’s second most popular specialty plate, are split 70/30, with 70% supporting the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s Marine Turtle Protection Program and 30% going to the Sea Turtle License Plate Grant (STLPG), administered by Sea Turtle Conservancy (STC). The grant funds research, education, and habitat conservation projects benefiting Florida’s sea turtles.
Staff is requesting authorization to apply for an estimated $8,600 in STLPG funding for FY 2027/28 to support the educational outreach effort of updated interpretive signage. STLPG applications for the FY 2027/28 funding cycle are due on November 6, 2026. If awarded, the grant would provide 100% cost-reimbursement for the hard costs incurred for this project outside of Staff time.
The goal of this project is to increase public awareness of sea turtles and their nesting habitat while providing visitors and residents with a permanent, onsite educational resource, in accordance with the HCP.
title: Requesting Permission to Submit a Sea Turtle License Plate Grant Application for Interpretive Sea Turtle Conservation Signage

description:
The Indian River County Department of Utility Services (County) operates the Hobart Water Production Facility (WPF) to provide potable water service to its customers. The WPF has a treatment capacity of 11.4 million gallons per day (MGD) and an average daily flow of approximately 7.0 MGD. The facility’s raw water supply is obtained from the Upper Floridan Aquifer through nine (9) groundwater wells located both on and off the WPF site.
Raw water from the wells is conveyed to the WPF through two (2) 20-inch-diameter pipelines. Each pipeline is reduced to 16 inches in diameter before entering the sand strainer system manufactured by Hydac International. The sand strainers provide initial pretreatment by removing coarse sand and other larger particulates from the raw water. The strained water is then combined into a single 24-inch-diameter raw water pipeline, which conveys the flow to the membrane treatment process. A static mixer is located within the 24-inch pipeline immediately upstream of the membrane treatment process building to facilitate chemical pretreatment.
The existing sand strainers are designed to operate automatically and are equipped with a self cleaning function. When the differential pressure across the strainer mesh reaches a preset value, the system automatically initiates a backwash cycle to remove accumulated solids and maintain appropriate hydraulic performance. Operational staff at the Hobart Water Production Facility (WPF) have identified issues with the existing sand strainer system. The primary concern is excessive pressure loss across the strainers during higher flow conditions, typically when flows exceed approximately 7.5 million gallons per day (MGD). Actual field measured pressure losses across the strainers have been significantly greater than the losses estimated by the manufacturer. The resulting reduction in pressure at the membrane feed pumps is particularly pronounced during backwash operations and can adversely affect reliable WPF operation.
To address the Hobart Sand Strainer staff desire to undertake the Work Order No. 5 for Tetra Tech, Inc. for Sand Strainer Evaluation and Design for Hobart Water Production Facility Sand Strainer Improvements, Project ID 12.26.524.
title: Approval of Work Order No. 5 for Tetra Tech, Inc. for Sand Strainer Evaluation and Design for Hobart Water Production Facility Sand Strainer Improvements, IRCDUS Project ID: 12.26.524

description: Beginning in 1990 and continuing to present, except for the period of time from 2009 through 2014 when the program was discontinued due to a lack of funding from the economic downturn, Indian River County (IRC) has participated in a Cost-Share program with the St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD) to plug abandoned artesian wells county-wide, including wells on private property (subject to authorization from the private landowner). As a result of the program, numerous free-flowing abandoned artesian wells within the County have been properly plugged, conserving millions of gallons of groundwater daily and helping prevent contamination of the groundwater supply. Uncontrolled free-flowing wells also have the potential for carrying pollutants (including elevated amounts of nitrogen and phosphorus) in overland flows ultimately ending up in the Indian River Lagoon.

description:
The Florida Legislature has appropriated funds for the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to provide financial support to coastal counties for the removal of qualified biological debris from the shoreline, reducing impacts from red tide or other harmful algae blooms. In Florida, red tide (Karenia brevis) produces toxins causing fish kills leading to biological debris accumulation on shorelines, potentially impacting tourism and local economies.
This Biological Debris Removal Grant is made available only to coastal counties within Florida and allocates $100,000 for each qualifying County. Since there was no formal application process and Indian River County qualifies geographically, FDEP staff has provided the grant agreement to Indian River County for consideration. If accepted, this grant would enable the County to seek reimbursement funding from the FDEP for the removal of qualifying biological debris from impacted coastlines through December 31, 2026, should mitigation be required.
Staff is requesting the Board of County Commissioners accept Grant agreement RT039 that supports qualified biological debris removal efforts on public shorelines in Indian River County. As a grant requirement, the County would be required to submit documentation of the biological debris contamination associated with red tide or other nuisance marine algae to FDEP for approval prior to any removal activities. The grant would provide the County with 100% cost reimbursement after the removal of biological debris is documented and submitted.
title: Acceptance of FDEP Biological Debris Removal Grant RT039

description:
Jungle Trail runs along the east bank of the Indian River Lagoon from approximately Old Winter Beach Road north through the Town of Orchid until it ends at its intersection with Highway A-1-A near Seaview Drive. It has been recognized as a Florida Greenway and also a historic and scenic road. In 2003, Jungle Trail was listed on the National Register of Historic Places by the United States Department of Interior. The trail has played an important part of the County’s local history by providing access to Jones Pier, the Captain Forster Preserve, to Pelican Island Wildlife Refuge and several citrus groves that were marketed as Jungle Trail Fruit.
In 2016 the County entered agreement with Michael and Sue Stutzke to use their trademarked Jungle Trail Fruit Co. fruit box labels and Historic Jungle Trail logo on advertising, trail markers, and other materials. The logos have remained part of the branding of the area since that time. The original agreement expired earlier this year and Mr. Stutzke reached out to the County desiring a longer-term renewal of 50 years. The Agreement has been updated to reflect this, and a few other changes.
title: Consideration of Renewing Jungle Trail Logo Agreement

description:
In January 2007, the Board of County Commissioners acquired the historic Archie Smith Fish House under the County’s environmental lands program. The subject waterfront property consists of approximately 1.15 acres located north of the intersection of Jackson Street and Indian River Drive in the City of Sebastian.
The property includes a dock, and prior to 2022, also included an icehouse extending over sovereign submerged lands of the Indian River Lagoon. The icehouse floor began to collapse in December 2021, and for safety reasons the entire icehouse was demolished in early 2022. The Board has authorized staff to proceed with replacement of the icehouse with an overwater pavilion.
Because the submerged lands are state sovereign lands, the County executed a sovereignty submerged lands lease with the State (Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund) in conjunction with property acquisition. The State submerged land lease is now up for renewal. To that end, attached is a copy of the 5-year lease renewal document for the Board’s approval consideration.
title: Approval of State Sovereignty Lands Fee Waived Lease 5-Year Renewal for the Archie Smith Fish House

description:
St. Francis Manor of Vero Beach, Florida, Inc. is a Florida Not-for-Profit Corporation that provides low-income housing and has been leasing from the County for more than 5 decades. On August 8, 1973, St. Francis Manor entered into an agreement to lease land from the county and proposed constructing an apartment facility for low-income disabled and senior citizens of Indian River County.
Since the signing of the original lease in 1973, the County and St. Francis Manor have agreed to ten (10) amendments to the lease and are described below.
• The First Amendment was executed on February 6, 1980, and added adjoining land to the Lease for the construction of an assisted living facility.
• The Second Amendment was executed on July 27, 1993, and gave permission for St. Francis Manor to refinance their mortgage for an interest rate advantage and for additions or improvements.
• The Third Amendment was entered into on September 19, 1994, and added a reverter clause stating that if an assisted living facility was not built on the additional lands included in the First Amendment 5 years from the date of the Third Amendment, the additional leased property would return to the County.
• The Fourth Amendment was agreed to and signed October 12, 1999, and extended the allotted time to construct the assisted living facility
• The Fifth Amendment was executed on February 7, 2006, and removed the reverter clause that was established in the Third Amendment and added all additional land to the original lease as the plan for an assisted living facility was abandoned for more apartments.
• The Sixth Amendment dated May 1, 2012, added additional land to the lease and removed the requirements for “carpeted floors” and “one hot meal a day” from the original lease.
• The Seventh Amendment was entered into on October 9, 2012, and changed the yearly rental amount from $1,000 per year to $1 per year. This amendment also forgave any unpaid rent.
• The Eighth Amendment was executed June 4, 2013, and added the “Old Jail Site” parcel, except for a tower and its accompanying easement, to the lease for the construction and improvement of the parcel. The Eighth Amendment also added time constraints for construction.

description:
Each year, Indian River County receives transit operating assistance under 49 USC Ch. 53, Section 5311 (also known as the Formula Grants for Rural Areas program) through the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT). These grant funds have been passed through to the Senior Resource Association (SRA), Indian River County’s designated transit service provider.
According to federal regulations, Formula Grants for Rural Areas funds may be used to provide transit service to rural or small urban areas. Such transit service includes fixed route service (GoLine) and demand-response service (Community Coach).
Earlier this year, the Board approved a Section 5311 grant application for FY 2026/27 at its August 4, 2026 meeting. Since then, FDOT informed County staff that a modification was needed to the Authorizing Resolution that was provided to FDOT with the grant application (see below):
“WHEREAS, Indian River County, as the designated recipient of federal and state public transportation funding, must be the recipient of those funds on behalf of the Senior Resource Association...”
Although this language has been consistent with previous Authorizing Resolutions for 5311 grant applications dating back to 2009, FDOT has notified County staff that the clause shown in strikethrough above must be removed from the resolution prior to issuance of the grant agreement. The requested change will not have any practical impact on the operation of Indian River County’s public transportation system by its contractor, Senior Resource Association.
title: Request for Authorization to Submit an Application for Section 5311 Grant for Rural Transit Operating Assistance Funds

description:
This item requests adoption of an ordinance that establishes a new section of the code entitled, “Expedited Permitting for Economic Development and Affordable Housing” within Chapter 902 of the Land Development Regulations.
The Board of County Commissioners previously provided policy direction to formalize expedited permitting for affordable housing and targeted economic development projects through two separate actions. On November 18, 2025, the Board adopted Resolution No. 2025-071, approving the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee Incentives Review and Recommendation Report. On January 27, 2026, the Board adopted the Indian River County Economic Development Strategic Action Plan.
Both documents recommend implementation of an expedited permitting process for qualifying affordable housing and economic development projects. The proposed ordinance formalizes eligibility criteria, procedures, and review timeframes for these projects within the County Code.
The Economic Development Council (EDC) considered the draft ordinance on July 21, 2026, and voted unanimously to approve the ordinance concept and directed staff to proceed with additional internal review and the required public hearings. The EDC subsequently reviewed the final draft and reaffirmed its support on September 15, 2026.
The Planning and Zoning Commission held a hearing on the ordinance on September 10, 2026, and determined the proposed ordinance was consistent with the Indian River County Comprehensive Plan; furthermore, the Commission unanimously recommended adoption of the Ordinance.
title: Ordinance to create Section 902.13, Chapter 902, County Code, Titled Expedited Permitting for Economic Development and Affordable Housing

description:
This item is for consideration of an Ordinance that revises Title XI, Chapter 1100, Indian River County Code, entitled Economic Development Ad Valorem Tax Exemption.
A local government’s authority to grant tax exemptions for economic development is provided in §196.1995, Florida Statutes. Indian River County’s Ad Valorem Tax Exemption was approved in 2010 by voter referendum for a ten-year period and was then codified under Ordinance No. 2010-014. Subsequently, the program was reaffirmed by the voter referendum in 2020 for an additional ten-years under Ordinance No. 2020-08.
Since Indian River County’s ability to provide an economic development tax exemption program is sanctioned in Florida Statutes, Chapter 1100 of the County Code is intended to reflect statutory requirements, process, and qualifications for the local tax exemption program. Much of Chapter 1100, Indian River County Code reflects the 2010 Florida Statutes, when the economic development exemption was first adopted by the County. After 2010, there was a substantive revision of §196.012, F.S. As such, Chapter 1100, County Code, should be updated to reflect the current statutory definitions for a business to qualify for and receive a local tax exemption.
title: Ordinance to Amend Title XI, Chapter 1100, Economic Development Tax Exemption

description:
This is the first of two public hearings required by Florida Statute Section 163.3225 for the approval of an amendment to the Emerson Oaks Developer's Agreement.The second public hearing is scheduled for October 20, 2026.
Emerson Oaks is a proposed residential planned development consisting of 171 Single Family lots to be located at the southwest corner of 43rd Avenue SW and 13th Street SW. This project is proposed to be constructed in 3 phases. Phase 1A consists of the model home row (seven lots), the project entrance on 13th Street SW, and the adjacent stormwater pond. Phase 1B will include 70 lots, the amenity center, and infrastructure commensurate with this phase. Phase 2 will include 94 lots (the remainder of the residential development), the project entrance on 17th Street SW, and the necessary utilities needed to support the phase 2 homes.
The original developer's agreement for this development was approved by the Board of County Commissioners on November 4, 2025. (Original Agreement attached hereto for reference.)
The developer was in the process of performing their duties under the original developer's agreement when they were approached by the Public Works Department with a request to add additional items that would otherwise be the County's responsibility — primarily the widening and paving of roads near the development.
County projects, particularly roadway projects, can be more costly because the county is required to go out to bid for project engineering and construction, along with mobilization and other associated costs for the improvements. By having the developer who is already mobilized in the area and working on their own portion of the project take over and do the county's portion, the county will save money because the developer can negotiate for cheaper prices and reduce mobilization costs. By doing the work on behalf of the county, the developer benefits by having all the areas near their developments being updated and ready to sell without having to sell homes during the counties construction period. This also benefits the public in that there will only be one construction period in that area instead of two separate construction periods in that area. This amendment to the original developer's agreement was staff initiated to attempt to obtain those benefits on behalf of the county and its current and future residents.
The cost estimate and scope of work that are to be completed by the developer are attached to the amended developers agreement as Exhibits "E" and "F." They have been approved by the county engineering division and are what the reimbursement to the developer is based on.
The change for the scope of work and reimbursement, along with the change in date of the agreement are the sole changes to the original developer's agreement.
title: First Public Hearing for First Amendment to Developers Agreement Between Pulte Home Company, LLC and Indian River County - Emerson Oaks PD

description:
The proposed LDR amendments being presented for the BCC’s consideration address xeriscaping, density bonuses for affordable and workforce housing developments, and reductions to certain landscaping requirements for qualifying affordable housing developments.
Staff proposes amending Chapter 901 to add a definition for xeriscaping. Xeriscaping is a water-conserving method of landscaping designed to reduce or eliminate the need for supplemental irrigation through the use of drought-tolerant and native plants, efficient irrigation methods, and moisture-retaining mulch.
The proposed ordinance also amends Chapter 914 to establish density bonus provisions for developments providing affordable and/or workforce housing. In addition, Chapter 926 is proposed to be amended to provide a process by which qualifying affordable housing development utilizing one-hundred (100) percent xeriscaping may request reductions to certain landscape and buffer requirements.
These amendments are proposed as a single ordinance. The Board of County Commissioners is to consider the proposed LDR amendments and make a motion to adopt, adopt with modifications, or deny the proposed ordinance.
title: Consideration of Staff-Initiated Land Development Regulation (LDR) Amendments to Chapter 901 Regarding Definitions, Chapter 914 Regarding Regulations for Site Plan Review and Approval Procedures, and Chapter 926 Regarding Regulations for Landscape and Buffer Regulations

description:
The Beach Preservation Plan (BPP) serves as the County's long-term, science-based framework for managing our 22.4 miles of Atlantic coastline. The original BPP was adopted by the Board of County Commissioners (Board) in 1988 and has since been periodically updated to incorporate advances in data, science, and technology, with updates completed in 1998, 2002, 2008, 2015, and 2019.
On May 7, 2024, the Board authorized work on the latest update to the BPP. Over the past two years, staff from the Coastal Engineering Division and our consulting team have evaluated extensive datasets on historical and current beach conditions, coastline risks, and coastal management practices to develop a robust update to the BPP. The primary objective of this update was to assess the effectiveness of historical coastal management actions within each planning Sector and to provide tailored recommendations for future management. This update includes 11 Sections addressing historical coastal conditions, sea level rise and water levels, recent beach condition analyses, sand resources, environmental and biological resources, coastal development and its economic impacts, risk analysis, beach management strategies, community outreach, and a summary of recommendations. The main document is supported by nine (9) comprehensive technical appendices that provide detailed analyses of the underlying datasets.
On May 5, 2026 Staff and engineering consultants presented the draft BPP 2026 Update to the Board. The public was invited to provide comments on the draft BPP between April 14, 2026 and May 19, 2026. Since the presentation on May 5, 2026, no significant changes were made to the BPP 2026 Update, except for the addition of Section 10- Community Outreach, which summarizes public outreach efforts and comments received. Following the public comment period, a total of 82 comments were submitted. Appendix I contains all 82 public comments and the prepared responses from the County.
The BPP 2026 Update is now complete, and staff are requesting the Board’s final approval to adopt the Beach Preservation Plan 2026 Update. The final BPP and Appendices are available on the County’s website: IndianRiver.gov/BPP.
title: Beach Preservation Plan 2026 Update – Final Adoption
