Indian River Citrus Crate Label Trail

description:
In July 2022, the Executive Director of the Vero Heritage Center contacted the Parks Maintenance Division regarding participation in the Florida Citrus Crate Label Trail through the installation of Citrus Crate Label signs on County-owned properties with a documented connection to Indian River County's citrus heritage. Initial discussions focused on identifying historically appropriate locations, including Jones' Pier Conservation Area, Captain Forster Hammock Preserve, and Hallstrom Farmstead Conservation Area. Other sites, such as Kroegel Homestead, were excluded because they lacked a direct historical association with the citrus industry (Heather Stapleton email dated July 7, 2022). Based on those discussions, the first two Citrus Crate Label signs were installed at Captain Forster Hammock Preserve and Jones' Pier Conservation Area on September 21, 2022.
In 2023, following a change in leadership at the Vero Heritage Center, the new Executive Director, Robyn Berry, contacted the County regarding the installation of an additional Citrus Crate Label sign at the Indian River County Courthouse. Correspondence with the Public Works Director advised that any installation at the Courthouse would require approval by the County Administrator. During these discussions, the Heritage Center shared its long-term vision of installing approximately 30 to 40 Citrus Crate Label signs throughout Indian River County as part of the statewide Florida Citrus Crate Label Trail. According to information provided by the Heritage Center, the program is sponsored in part by the Indian River County Tourist Development Council and local business sponsors.
Between 2023 and 2025, representatives of the Vero Heritage Center, including Brenda Burnette (Interim Executive Director and Board President) and Leslie McKenzie (Executive Director), continued coordinating directly with staff from various County departments and divisions to request placement of additional Citrus Crate Label signs on publicly owned properties. During this period, the Heritage Center also executed an agreement with the City of Vero Beach for installations at City-owned parks and public spaces. Within the County park system, the Parks Superintendent authorized installation of signs at Kiwanis-Hobart Lakeside Park (East), Kiwanis-Hobart Park (West), Wabasso Causeway Park, and Wabasso Beach Park. These installations approved administratively, were located within park property boundaries, and did not require right-of-way permits or other permitting. However, neither Board of County Commissioners approval nor County Administrator authorization was obtained for these installations.
In July 2025, the County Historian, Ruth Stanbridge, notified County staff of concerns regarding several recently installed Citrus Crate Label signs. Specifically, concerns were raised regarding the historical appropriateness of certain locations, and the potential for public confusion with the Florida Historical Marker Program. Unlike the Citrus Crate Label Trail, Florida Historical Markers are subject to a rigorous process including extensive historical research, documentation, and the markers are State approval through the Florida Historical Marker Program before installation.
title: Vero Beach Heritage Center Request for Citrus Crate Label Signage at Indian River County Parks and Conservation Areas

description:
The County’s Comprehensive Plan contains specific regulations for mixed-use planned developments in Chapter 2, Future Land Use Element, Policy 5.6. The County’s Land Development Regulations (LDRs) contain corresponding regulations for mixed-use planned developments in Section 915.20 (see Attachment 1).
The County’s mixed-use standards provide special development allowances within the SR 60/IRSC Preferred Location Area, which is generally located near the SR 60/58th Avenue Commercial/Industrial Node, the SR 60/66th Avenue intersection, and the Indian River State College campus. These allowances include a maximum project area of eighty (80) acres rather than forty (40) acres and an increased allowance for commercial uses of fifty (50) percent rather than twenty-five (25) percent.
The County’s LDRs also regulate maximum building height by zoning district. Generally, County zoning districts limit building height to thirty-five (35) feet, except within two established height exception areas. The first allows certain coastal hotel, motel, and resort developments to reach a maximum height of forty-five (45) feet if the property is located east of Highway A1A, zoned CG, and meets applicable design criteria. The second allows certain industrial and warehouse distribution buildings west of I-95 to reach a maximum height of eighty (80) feet when specified zoning, setback, site-size, and other design criteria are met. In addition to these generally applicable height provisions, the Cleveland Clinic Indian River Hospital previously received a site-specific variance allowing a maximum building height of one hundred thirty-four (134) feet, with an additional sixteen (16) feet permitted for an elevator structure, resulting in a maximum authorized height of one hundred fifty (150) feet for that specific site.
title: Developer Presentation and Discussion Concerning Regulations for a Hospital at State Road 60 and 66th Avenue Including Increased Building Height and Building Coverage

description: Sandridge Golf Club is entering an exciting new chapter with the construction of a state-of-the-art, 22,000-square-foot clubhouse that will redefine the guest experience and expand the Club's role as a premier destination in Indian River County. The new facility, currently in its final stages of construction, is anticipated to receive its Certificate of Occupancy on October 20, 2026. The clubhouse will feature a modern golf shop, a full-service restaurant with a commercial kitchen, a banquet facility capable of accommodating up to 200 guests with a dedicated catering kitchen, and a beautifully designed event lawn for outdoor gatherings. This transformational project represents far more than a new clubhouse—it positions Sandridge Golf Club as a year-round venue capable of hosting a diverse range of events beyond golf. In addition to serving golfers, the facility will attract weddings, receptions, corporate meetings, holiday parties, community events, expos, fundraisers, celebrations, and other private and public functions. The expanded amenities will create new revenue opportunities, strengthen community engagement, and establish Sandridge Golf Club as one of the Treasure Coast's premier destinations for golf, dining, and special events for years to come. In preparation for the opening of the restaurant and banquet facility at Sandridge Golf Club, Staff has prepared standardized pricing for banquet facility events.

The North Sebastian Phase 3 Septic-to-Sewer (S2S) conversions are currently underway, with Phase 1 and 2 having been completed in April 2019 and June 2023 respectively. The North Sebastian area encompasses an area generally described as having a western limit of US Highway 1, an eastern limit of the Indian River Lagoon, a northern limit of Indian River Drive connection to US Highway 1, and the southern limit as Main Street. To date, approximately 154 sewer connections have been completed.

description:
The Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) Program, formerly known as Section 8 Housing, is a federally funded program administered locally by the Indian River County Housing Services Division. The program assists very low- and extremely low-income households by providing rental subsidies for safe, decent, and affordable housing in the private rental market. The County does not own any HCV housing units; instead, it contracts with private landlords whose properties meet HUD’s Housing Quality Standards.
Federal regulations require that utility allowance rates, covering water, sewer, gas, electric, and propane, be reviewed and approved by the Board of County Commissioners annually by resolution. These rates represent the estimated average monthly cost of tenant-paid utilities for different unit sizes and are used in calculating the total housing assistance payment for each family.
For Fiscal Year 2027, Housing Services retained The Nelrod Company to conduct a local utility rate study. The study’s methodology follows HUD guidance, using current utility provider rates and average consumption data for the County. Staff reviewed and approved the final report, and the recommended utility rates are included as an attachment to the resolution. Upon Board approval, these rates will become effective October 1, 2026.
title: Approval of Resolution Establishing Utility Rates for Housing Choice Voucher Program for Fiscal Year 2027

description:
Indian River County Code designates the Deputy County Attorney as the County’s Fair Housing Coordinator. Among the County’s housing programs is the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) Program, formerly known as Section 8 Housing. Federal regulations require the Board of County Commissioners to approve, by resolution, the Housing Choice Voucher Program payment standards each year. These payment standards are established in relation to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) published Fair Market Rents (FMRs).
The HCV Program is a federally funded rental assistance program administered locally by the County’s Housing Services Division. While federal regulations establish program requirements, local demographics influence program administration. Indian River County has a significantly higher proportion of residents age 65 and older (approximately 36%) than the national average (approximately 18%). This demographic characteristic increases the demand for affordable housing options for low-income older adults. The program also serves veterans, persons with disabilities, and other low-income households.
The County owns no housing under this program. Instead, private landlords make their units available, and each unit must meet HUD's National Standards for the Physical Inspection of Real Estate (NSPIRE) before being approved for tenancy. In exchange for participating, landlords benefit from reliable Housing Assistance Payments (HAP) and potential tax advantages, while participating households obtain safe, decent, and affordable housing. Eligible households generally contribute between 30% and 40% of their adjusted monthly income toward rent and utilities, with the remaining eligible housing assistance paid directly to the landlord by the County on HUD's behalf. The program supports the County's Comprehensive Plan objective of ensuring access to housing for very low- and extremely low-income residents while generating administrative fee revenue from HUD to support program operations.
title: Approval of Resolution Establishing Payment Standards (Based on HUD’s Fair Market Rents) for Housing Choice Voucher Program for Fiscal Year 2027

description:
It is requested that the data herein presented be given formal consideration by the Board of County Commissioners at its regular meeting of September 15, 2026.
In the early 1990’s, the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program was created by the State of Florida. Through that program, the state collects documentary stamp tax revenue and allocates those funds to local governments to be used for affordable housing purposes.
On April 6, 1993, the Board of County Commissioners adopted the Indian River County Local Housing Assistance Plan (Ordinance #93-13). By adopting the plan and subsequently receiving Florida Housing Finance Corporation approval of the plan, Indian River County became eligible to receive State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program funds.
The purpose of the SHIP program is to provide affordable housing for income-qualified households. As structured, the county’s SHIP Program provides deferred payment and subordinated loans to eligible extremely low income, very low income, low income, and moderate-income households. Those loans are provided primarily for purchase assistance and rehabilitation assistance. As part of the SHIP purchase assistance program, private financial institutions provide principal mortgages, while SHIP loans are generally structured as soft second mortgages.
Since SHIP is a state-funded program, the SHIP program fiscal year (FY) is concurrent with the state fiscal year and runs from July 1 to June 30. Because SHIP funds provided in one fiscal year can be spent over a three fiscal year period, the county often has two or more years of SHIP funding active. For example, in the past year the county has expended funds from the following SHIP program fiscal year: FY 22/23 and FY 23/24, and encumbered funds from FY 24/25.
title: Consideration of Brownstone Affordable Housing, Ltd., application for SHIP New Construction Federal or State Programs Matching Loans

description:
On September 17, 2019, at the request of the Community Development Department, the Board waived the requirement for bids and authorized a direct agreement with the South-Central Planning and Development Commission (“SCPDC”) for their My Government Online (“MGO”) permitting software. Implementation was considered completed in October of 2022, but not all the anticipated models have been activated. The software is used mainly for building permits as all other departments did not support moving forward with utilizing MGO for their respective permitting types, for various reasons but mainly that they did not feel MGO performed efficiently and did not meet the needs of our external customers, therefore an alternative solution was requested.
A Task Force, led by the County Administration Ombudsman and comprised of approximately 30 members of the following divisions (Public Works-Land Development and Right of Way, Utilities, Building, Life Safety, Fire Prevention, Contractor Licensing, Planning and Development, Code Enforcement, Environmental Planning, and IT/GIS), developed a list of requirements for a new software solution.
On May 30, 2025, a Request for Information (RFI) was issued for a new software product, listing the requirements and desired functionality, with suppliers asked to indicate the extent to which their product met the requirements. A total of 22 responses to the questionnaires were received. The task force eliminated 14 submittals for not meeting minimum requirements or being suitable for the County’s needs. The remaining eight firms were asked follow-up and clarifying questions through the Procurement Division. Five firms were ultimately invited to participate in product demonstrations with the task force between November 2025-June 2026. Those 5 firms were: Govwell, Sages, Intuitive Municipal Solutions (iMS), OpenGov and MGO. After the demonstrations, the task force, through the Procurement Division, submitted additional follow-up questions to all firms. Discussions about data migration & conversion, AI capabilities, financial payment processes, cyber security, GIS capabilities, plan review software capabilities were had and evaluated.
Initially, the majority of the Task Force recommended GovWell to be the best solution for the County, discussions related to the final scope of work and agreement commenced and during a very thorough due diligence process it was determined that GovWell may not be the ideal software system for development review, this decision was made in part by reaching out to other jurisdictions who currently use GovWell and asking what they did and did not like about the system, coordinating meetings with GovWell and GIS/I.T., and Finance to understand the intricacies of the non-customer facing portion of the system (back-end) and our task force members research on how many modules those jurisdictions that had GovWell used and their capabilities.
The Task Force was reconvened again, and discussed several development review software systems, including Accela and Tyler. Staff also reached out to surrounding municipalities, contractors, and engineers for input on systems they have worked with. We discussed GovWell and some of our concerns, ultimately the Task Force agreed to conduct additional demos with both iMS and OpenGov.
Throughout the evaluation process, iMS consistently demonstrated that it understands the needs of Florida local governments, this is important because building permitting relies on the Florida Building Code, not the Southern Building Code (SBC) or International Building Code (IBC) like other states. The system offers flexibility to adapt to the County's processes without requiring the manual processes that are now occurring with MGO. Simple process improvements can be made by designated county staff administrators versus waiting for the company to make them. iMS also provides for unlimited data migration thereby allowing the county to utilize one system instead of three and a fully integrated platform that allows all county departments, City of Vero Beach & Department of Health to work together in one system, creating a more efficient permitting process for both staff, the development community, and our public.
title: Approval of Permitting Software Selection and Agreements

description:
The U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Justice Programs, Bureau of Justice Assistance has announced two FY 2026 competitive funding opportunities that align with Indian River County’s ongoing efforts to strengthen Mental Health Court and improve coordination among the County’s behavioral health, substance use, public safety, judicial, and community partners.
The first opportunity is the FY 2026 Comprehensive Opioid, Stimulant, and Substance Use Site Based Program, commonly referred to as COSSUP. The County is eligible to request up to $1.3 million over a 36-month project period. The program supports comprehensive approaches to addressing substance use and overdose risk, including treatment and recovery services, court-based interventions, recovery support, housing, transportation, reentry, and related coordination and data activities.
The second opportunity is the FY 2026 Public Safety and Mental Health Initiative. The County is eligible to request up to $3 million over a 36-month project period. This program supports coordinated responses to individuals with mental health and substance use needs who interact with law enforcement and the criminal justice system. Eligible activities may include crisis stabilization, behavioral health and substance use treatment, recovery services, reentry support, coordination with the justice system, and technology and data improvements intended to improve continuity of care.
The two funding opportunities address related but distinct needs within the County’s behavioral health and justice system. Staff proposes developing separate applications with clearly defined scopes, budgets, populations, and activities to ensure that federal funds are complementary and do not duplicate services or costs.
Applications for COSSUP must be submitted through Grants.gov by September 24, 2026, with full application due through JustGrants by October 1, 2026. Applications for the Public Safety and Mental Health Initiative must be submitted through Grants.gov by September 25, 2026, with full application due through JustGrants by October 2, 2026.

description:
The County is self-insured in its Group Health Insurance Program and carries a policy that reimburses the County for claims that exceed a specific limit. This type of policy is called a stop loss policy, excess loss policy, or reinsurance policy. The County’s current stop loss policy is with Highmark and has an individual stop loss deductible of $300,000 for individual claims and an aggregating specific stop loss deductible of $100,000. The County also carries aggregate stop loss coverage for the entire medical/pharmacy plan. Below is an explanation of individual stop loss, aggregating specific stop loss deductible, and aggregated stop loss coverages.Individual Stop Loss Specific Deductible (ISL) – IRC’s liability on everyone on the plan (currently ISL is $300k)
Aggregating Specific Deductible (ASD) – For any ISL claims in excess of $300k, IRC takes the liability for an additional $100k in claims. This can either be satisfied by one member in excess of $300k, or multiple members. The purpose of an aggregating specific deductible is to lower premiums paid to the stop-loss carrier in exchange for the plan sponsor potentially paying a bit more in claims throughout the policy period.
Aggregated Stop Loss (ASL) – ASL protects the plan from unexpected, catastrophically high claims that exceed the limits of potential reserves. The aggregate stop loss coverage provides a $1M policy to IRC in the event the claims paid in the plan year exceeded 125% of expected claims.
The current annual premium for the stop loss policy with Highmark is $1,200,271 with a total fixed cost liability of $1,300,271 inclusive of the aggregating specific deductible of $100K. The monthly premium is based on a per employee per month (PEPM) rate of $56.57 per 1,765 lives. The actual monthly premium amount fluctuates based on monthly enrollment in the health plan. The current stop loss policy has a renewal rate cap of 40%.
Stop loss experience through June 2026 reflects a loss ratio of 207% with 9 individuals exceeding the individual stop loss deductible of $300K.
Our benefits consultant and broker, Lockton Companies, sent a request for stop loss proposals to 11 carriers. Our current carrier, Highmark (HM), provided a firm proposal. Berkshire Hathaway and Nationwide declined to provide firm proposals due to uncompetitive rates and laser liability. Sun Life, Option, Swiss Re, Symetra, TMHCC, Voya, and Wellpoint carriers declined to quote due to uncompetitive rates and ongoing liability.
After receiving the renewal quote, the County received notification that the Sheriffs Office was leaving the County group insurance program and electing separate group insurance coverage for its members. As a result, the County obtained an updated renewal quote from Highmark to reflect the change in covered lives which are now projected to be 1,298. Attached is the Fiscal Year 2026/2027 Stop Loss Marketing Analysis for October 1, 2026, effective date. This package includes the market information, benchmarking information, Monte Carlo Modeler, and pricing grid comparison.
The updated HM firm renewal quote reflects a 40% increase in PEPM premium at $79.33 PEPM or $1,235,644 per 1,298 lives with a total fixed cost liability of $1,335,644 inclusive of the aggregating specific deductible of $100K. Options to increase the individual specific deductible from $300K to $325K/$350K/$400K/$450K/$500K, were also provided at a lower premium than the renewal premium. However, Lockton’s analysis does not support increasing the individual specific deductible over $300K.
title: Approval of Stop Loss Renewal with Highmark for Group Health Plan Fiscal Year 2026/2027

attachments.name: Resolution to Modify the IRCDUS Water Impact Fee Rate

description:
Indian River County Department of Utility Services (IRCDUS) operates as an enterprise fund with its primary source of income being service fees and usage (volume) charges from its customers. Additional funding comes from miscellaneous charges and impact fees.
In 2023, IRCDUS engaged a third-party utility rate consultant, Stantec Consulting Services, Inc. (Stantec) to review and recommend service fees, usage and impact fee rate changes for IRCDUS.
On August 22, 2024, IRCDUS conducted a public workshop for the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners (BCC) to review the results of the Utility Rate Study completed by Stantec. Between August 22, 2024, and September 23, 2024, multiple public presentations of the Utility Rate Study results were conducted recommending adoption of a two-step rate increase effective January 1, 2025 and October 1, 2025.
In addition, the presentations discussed the results of the impact fee evaluation, which included a proposal to increase the water impact fee by $706. However, the “Florida Impact Fee Act” (F.S. 163.31801) restricts impact fee increases to no more than 50% of the current impact fee. Furthermore, the “Act” requires any increase greater than 25% be spread out in equal installments over a four-year period.
As a result, the study recommended an impact fee increase of $652 spread out in four equal installments of $163 in each of the following four years. Each presentation also provided the public an opportunity to ask questions and make comments on the proposed rate and impact fee changes. Finally, in late September 2024, the BCC conducted a public hearing to review and adopt two years of rate and impact fee increases that were effective January 1, 2025 and October 1, 2025.
title: Public Hearing to Discuss and Consider the Fiscal Year 2026/2027 Utility Services Impact Fee Rates for the Indian River County Department of Utility Services

description:
The Legislature in 2026 proposed and passed Senate Bill 488. This particular bill made changes to the requirements for permitting providers of communications services in public rights-of-way under Florida Statute Section 337.401. The changes included the following: Requirement to allow for an unlimited number of permits to be issued by a local government under a single form of security.
Pre-empting local governments from limiting the number of permits issued to a provider in any way, including project size, as well as the number of open permits or applications, so long as the permit is closed out within 45 days after the provider's completion of work.
Pre-empting local governments from requiring cash to be an acceptable form of security.
Pre-empting local governments from requiring a provider to perform a survey to locate any facilities except it's own or the right-of-way boundary.
Pre-empting local governments from requiring landscaping, landscaping maintenance, or vegetation maintenance other than what is required for restoration of the right-of-way.
The new statutory provisions/changes go into effect on October 1, 2026. In order to be in compliance with the new required changes, the attached proposed ordinance amendments are being suggested. The amendments will allow for all the required changes by the new law to be put into place. It will also allow for an update of the images of the construction standards that are no longer relevant or in place, as well as a few minor corrections/updates that correct dates and spelling.

description:
The Indian River County Landfill has a voluntary landfill gas collection system, Landfill Gas Collection and Control System (GCCS), that requires routine and non-routine operations and maintenance (O&M) as well as various expansions. The general purpose of the GCCS is to capture the methane gas to reduce odors, reduce the risk of fires and to reduce it to the less harmful carbon dioxide via flaring in the short run, and to ultimately facilitate the sale of the landfill gas to NoPetro EcoDistrict (NED) for its renewable natural gas (RNG) project.
SWDD staff are finalizing a GCCS O&M Request for Proposals (RFP), which is anticipated to be posted and awarded this year. As there is no formal agreement for O&M, we are utilizing our agreement with Republic Services to have them subcontract with Integrity Environmental Solutions to provide O&M services on a per item basis. These services are being overseen by SWDD staff and NoPetro.
On June 2, 2026, the SWDD Board waived the requirement for bids and authorized the Procurement Manager to issue a purchase order (PO) for the GCCS Operation Monitoring & Maintenance with Integrity Environmental Solutions for a six-month cost not to exceed $241,998. This included providing O&M services of the landfill gas well field at a monthly cost of $27,833.00 plus a $75,000 contingency for non-routine work.
As the RFP for the GCCS system is still being finalized, staff is requesting an extension of the PO to Integrity for an additional six months as well as to add a change order to the PO to add O&M of the High Pressure Gas Skid.
title: Change Order to Integrity for O&M of IRC Landfill Gas Collection and Control System

description:
On July 16, 2019, the Solid Waste Disposal District (SWDD) and Indian River Eco District, LLC entered into a Landfill Gas Agreement for the refinement of the gases produced at the landfill into renewable natural gas. The Agreement has been assigned to Nopetro Eco District LLC (NED), a Florida limited liability company, and has had four amendments, the most recent being heard by the Board on January 23, 2024.
Section 3.3C of the 3rd Amendment includes provision for Commercial and Environmental Improvement (CEI) projects that may be proposed by NED and that SWDD may elect to jointly fund but have no obligation to do so. The section does require NED to issue a notice to SWDD of the terms of the agreement for the CEI project to include respective responsibilities for such improvements.
On June 16, 2026, the SWDD Board approved a CEI project for the installation of an interim horizontal gas collection well network in Segment 3, Cells 2 and 3. That project was fully financed by NED with no financial obligation to SWDD. Installation began July 13, 2026, and was completed August 15, 2026, and those wells are currently being commissioned.
On August 21, 2026, NED sent the attached letter giving notice of a second CEI project – replacement of eighteen (18) vertical landfill gas extraction wells in Segments 1, 2 and 3. NED states that these wells are underperforming because leachate cannot drain, the leachate recovery pumps are stuck or inoperable, or the perforated pipe is blocked, and that replacing them will improve both leachate removal and gas recovery.
NED's letter as revised asks that the District consider sharing the cost of the project on a 50/50 basis. It does not ask the Board to commit District funds at this meeting.
title: Request by Nopetro Eco-District, LLC for Commercial and Environmental Improvements for Landfill Gas Collection - Vertical Well Redrills

description:
The County is self-insured in its Group Health Insurance Program and carries a policy that reimburses the County for claims that exceed a specific limit. This type of policy is called a stop loss policy, excess loss policy, or reinsurance policy. The County’s current stop loss policy is with Highmark and has an individual stop loss deductible of $300,000 for individual claims and an aggregating specific stop loss deductible of $100,000. The County also carries aggregate stop loss coverage for the entire medical/pharmacy plan. Below is an explanation of individual stop loss, aggregating specific stop loss deductible, and aggregated stop loss coverages.
Individual Stop Loss Specific Deductible (ISL) – IRC’s liability on everyone on the plan (currently ISL is $300k)
Aggregating Specific Deductible (ASD) – For any ISL claims in excess of $300k, IRC takes the liability for an additional $100k in claims. This can either be satisfied by one member in excess of $300k, or multiple members. The purpose of an aggregating specific deductible is to lower premiums paid to the stop-loss carrier in exchange for the plan sponsor potentially paying a bit more in claims throughout the policy period.
Aggregated Stop Loss (ASL) – ASL protects the plan from unexpected, catastrophically high claims that exceed the limits of potential reserves. The aggregate stop loss coverage provides a $1M policy to IRC in the event the claims paid in the plan year exceeded 125% of expected claims.
The current annual premium for the stop loss policy with Highmark is $1,200,271 with a total fixed cost liability of $1,300,271 inclusive of the aggregating specific deductible of $100K. The monthly premium is based on a per employee per month (PEPM) rate of $56.57 per 1,765 lives. The actual monthly premium amount fluctuates based on monthly enrollment in the health plan. The current stop loss policy has a renewal rate cap of 40%.
Stop loss experience through June 2026 reflects a loss ratio of 207% with 9 individuals exceeding the individual stop loss deductible of $300K.
Our benefits consultant and broker, Lockton Companies, sent a request for stop loss proposals to 11 carriers. Our current carrier, Highmark (HM), provided a firm proposal. Berkshire Hathaway and Nationwide declined to provide firm proposals due to uncompetitive rates and laser liability. Sun Life, Option, Swiss Re, Symetra, TMHCC, Voya, and Wellpoint carriers declined to quote due to uncompetitive rates and ongoing liability.
Attached is the Fiscal Year 2026/2027 Stop Loss Marketing Analysis for October 1, 2026, effective date. This package includes the market information, benchmarking information, Monte Carlo Modeler, and pricing grid comparison.
HM provided a firm renewal quote reflecting a 40% increase in PEPM premium at $79.34 PEPM or $1,680,421 per 1,765 lives with a total fixed cost liability of $1,780,421 inclusive of the aggregating specific deductible of $100K. This is a total increase of $480,150, or 40%, annually. Options to increase the individual specific deductible from $300K to $325K/$350K/$400K/$450K/$500K, as well as proposals with a $500k laser on one of the high-cost claimants, are also provided at a lower premium than the renewal premium. However, Lockton’s analysis does not support increasing the individual specific deductible over $300K or adding a $500K laser.
title: Approval of Stop Loss Renewal with Highmark for Group Health Plan Fiscal Year 2026/2027

The clubhouse will feature a modern golf shop, a full-service restaurant with a commercial kitchen, a banquet facility capable of accommodating up to 200 guests with a dedicated catering kitchen, and a beautifully designed event lawn for outdoor gatherings. This transformational project represents far more than a new clubhouse—it positions Sandridge Golf Club as a year-round venue capable of hosting a diverse range of events beyond golf. In addition to serving golfers, the facility will attract weddings, receptions, corporate meetings, holiday parties, community events, expos, fundraisers, celebrations, and other private and public functions. The expanded amenities will create new revenue opportunities, strengthen community engagement, and establish Sandridge Golf Club as one of the Treasure Coast's premier destinations for golf, dining, and special events for years to come. In preparation for the opening of the restaurant and banquet facility at Sandridge Golf Club, Staff has prepared standardized pricing and a set of policies (a binding agreement) for banquet facility events.
title: Sandridge Event Agreement & Venue Pricing

attachments.name: SHIP Funds and Applicants Information Summary

description:
It is requested that the data herein presented be given formal consideration by the Board of County Commissioners at its regular meeting of August 18, 2026.
In the early 1990’s, the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program was created by the State of Florida. Through that program, the state collects documentary stamp tax revenue and allocates those funds to local governments to be used for affordable housing purposes.
On April 6, 1993, the Board of County Commissioners adopted the Indian River County Local Housing Assistance Plan (Ordinance #93-13). By adopting the plan and subsequently receiving Florida Housing Finance Corporation approval of the plan, Indian River County became eligible to receive State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program funds.
The purpose of the SHIP program is to provide affordable housing for income-qualified households. As structured, the county’s SHIP Program provides low interest, deferred payment, and subordinated loans to eligible extremely low income, very low income, low income, and moderate-income households. Those loans are provided primarily for purchase assistance and rehabilitation assistance. As part of the SHIP purchase assistance program, private financial institutions provide principal mortgages, while SHIP loans are generally structured as soft second mortgages.
Since SHIP is a state-funded program, the SHIP program fiscal year (FY) is concurrent with the state fiscal year and runs from July 1 to June 30. Because SHIP funds provided in one fiscal year can be spent over a three fiscal year period, the county often has two or more years of SHIP funding active. For example, in the past year the county has expended funds from the following SHIP program fiscal year: FY 22/23 and FY 23/24, and encumbered funds from FY 24/25.
For each FY, SHIP funds consist of state allocations (unless funds are withheld or swept to fund other state purposes) and program income. Program income consists of SHIP loan repayments and interest earned. Attachment #1 shows historic SHIP fund information. That includes the number of loans provided to eligible applicants by fiscal year and by income category.
According to SHIP Program requirements, the county must submit an annual report for the closeout fiscal year (FY23/24) showing that all allocated SHIP funds were expended for that FY. That report must also include interim year data for interim year 1 (FY 24/25). A certification form for the report must be signed by the Chairperson of the Board of County Commissioners or his designee. For all previous fiscal years, closeout reports were previously submitted to and approved by the state. Attachment #2 to this staff report is the county’s SHIP Program FY 2023-2024 annual closeout report with interim year data for FY 2024-2025. The FY 2023-2024 final closeout annual report must be submitted to the state by September 15, 2026.
title: Consideration of the Indian River County SHIP Program 2026 Annual Report

description:
It is requested that the data herein presented be given formal consideration by the Board of County Commissioners at its regular meeting on August 18, 2026.
Pursuant to the requirements of Section 420.907, F.S., and Rule 67-37.005, Florida Administrative Code (FAC), the Board of County Commissioners approved the County’s first Local Housing Assistance Plan (Ordinance #93-13) on April 6, 1993. Subsequently, the Florida Housing Finance Corporation approved the County’s plan and authorized the disbursement of State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program funds.
According to Rule 67-37.005(2), the Florida Administrative Code, every three years, each local government receiving SHIP funds must submit a new Local Housing Assistance Plan (LHAP) to the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. Accordingly, the County’s plan was submitted in 1994, 1997, 2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018, 2021, and 2024.
In 2024, the Board of County Commissioners approved the County’s current 3-year plan. This agenda item reviews the proposed amendments to the current LHAP for FY 2024-2025, FY 2025-2026, and FY 2026-2027.SHIP Program Activity
Since its initial adoption in 1993, the County’s LHAP has been successful in directing assistance to eligible households within the county. The attached table (attachment #1) identifies the County’s SHIP allocations and the number of loans given to eligible applicants by fiscal year and by income category.
Since SHIP is a state-funded program, the SHIP program fiscal year (FY) is concurrent with the state fiscal year and runs from July 1 to June 30. Because SHIP funds provided in one fiscal year can be spent over a three fiscal year period, the county often has two or more years of SHIP funding active.
For each fiscal year (FY), SHIP funds consist of state allocations and program income. Program income includes SHIP loan repayments and interest earned. For FY 2024–25, full funding estimated at approximately $1.2 million was approved by the Legislature.
title: Consideration of the revised Indian River County Local Housing Assistance Plan for the Fiscal Years 2024-2025, 2025-2026, and 2026-2027

description:
For the past several years, the county has applied for and received transit operating assistance under the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Corridor Grant program. These grant funds have been passed through to the Senior Resource Association (SRA), Indian River County’s transit service provider.
FDOT Corridor Grant funds may be used for improving transit operations, such as realigning routes or increasing coverage areas. Since 2009, the County has used FDOT Corridor Grant funding for intercounty service to the Indian River State College (IRSC) Main Campus in Fort Pierce. Since 2014, this service has been provided through GoLine Route 15, which connects with three other GoLine routes (Routes 4, 6, and 7) at the Intergenerational Center. With a simple transfer, riders coming from the IRSC Mueller Campus, the Main Transit Hub, the Indian River Mall, Vero Beach Highlands, and other locations may travel to the IRSC Main Campus in St. Lucie County.
The current Public Transportation Grant Agreement (PTGA) with FDOT was executed on September 29, 2023 to continue intercity bus service via GoLine route 15. Through this grant, intercounty transit service to St. Lucie County is 100% funded by FDOT with no local contribution needed. The current grant provided three years of funding and expires later this year; this amendment will add an additional fourth year along with an increase in funding. Notably, this grant has provided $150,000 annually for the operation of Route 15. With this amendment, the funding assistance for FY2027 is being increased to $178,545 (see Attachment 2).
title: Amendment to the Public Transportation Grant Agreement (PTGA) with the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) for Intercounty Bus Service

description:
Indian River County completed the Sector 5 Hurricanes Ian and Nicole Beach and Dune Restoration Project (Project) in March 2026. The Project extended from north of Tracking Station Beach Park approximately 3.1 miles to south of the Riomar Golf Course and restored the beach and dune from losses associated with background erosion and Hurricanes Ian and Nicole impacts. The completed Project placed 115,901 cubic yards of beach-compatible sand and installed 117,500 native dune plants.
Permits issued by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) and the United States Army Corps of Engineers require the County to conduct post-construction monitoring of the completed Project. The monitoring will document Project performance and evaluate changes within the Project area in order to demonstrate compliance with applicable permit conditions.
On June 1, 2026, FDEP opened the application portal for FY 2027/28 Local Government Funding Request (LGFR) grants through the Beach Management Funding Assistance Program. The Program provides opportunities for State cost-share funding to eligible local governments for approved beach management activities, including project design, engineering and environmental studies, construction, and post-construction monitoring consistent with FDEP’s Strategic Beach Management Plan.
The County’s FY 2027/28 LGFR application requests partial State cost-share reimbursement for construction costs and future cost-share assistance with permit-required post-construction monitoring activities associated with the completed Sector 5 Project. Construction costs incurred along with post-construction monitoring are eligible for reimbursements and cost-sharing through FDEP’s Beach Management Funding Assistance Program.
The Project’s construction costs include the contract with Guettler Brothers Construction and APTIM’s workorder that provided engineering oversight. Permit-required post-construction monitoring is currently underway for this 2026 season which includes workorders for daily sea turtle surveys, hardbottom reef surveys physical beach profile surveys and weekly escarpment surveys. The construction permits required post-construction monitoring for 2026, 2027, and 2028. Combined construction and post-construction monitoring costs are estimated to be at a total cost of $5,972,022.57.
FEMA, through the Public Assistance Program, has previously obligated an estimated $2,422,801.00 toward the reimbursement of construction costs and 2026 post-construction monitoring due to damages sustained from Hurricanes Ian and Nicole within Sector 5. A current FDEP grant, 23IR2, has obligated $885,600 toward the reimbursement of construction costs and 2026 post-construction monitoring. The remaining $2,663,621.57 in estimated combined incurred and future costs is currently unsupported by an external funding program and represents eligible expenses for this current grant application.
Through the LGFR program requirements and based on available public access, the County’s Sector 5 Project qualifies for up to 46.65% State cost share on eligible expenses. With the allowable cost share under the LGFR program, the application requests $1,242,579.46 in State funds, which would reduce the County’s expense to approximately $1,421,042.11 after existing grants and obligations (FEMA and 23IR2) are accounted for.
As a result of a July 31, 2026 application deadline and the Board of County Commissioners (Board) meeting schedule, there was insufficient time to obtain the Board’s customary authorization before submitting the application. On July 28, 2026, to pursue this state cost-share funding opportunity, the County Administrator authorized staff to submit the application, subject to subsequent consideration and approval by the Board.
FDEP’s Beach Management Funding Assistance Program requires a funding resolution from the Local Sponsor demonstrating support for the project, the County’s willingness to serve as Local Sponsor, its ability to provide the full local cost share, and identification of the local funding source. The proposed Resolution is attached for Board consideration. Approval of the Resolution and submitted application does not obligate the County to accept a grant if awarded. If funding is awarded, the grant agreement and any necessary budget amendments will be presented to the Board for consideration.
title: Grant Application for Funding Assistance from the State of Florida Beach Management Funding Assistance Program-FY 2027/28

description:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) has included the Indian River County Federal Shore Protection Project on a proposed list of inactive Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) projects being considered for de-authorization. The project was identified in the Federal Register notice published on May 21, 2026 and appears on page 6 of the Proposed De-authorization List under Docket No. COE-2026-0034. Following review of the project history and the potential consequences of deauthorization, Natural Resources Department Staff concluded preserving the current federal authorization may align with the County's beach management objectives and retains the potential for future cost-sharing opportunities.
De-authorization would eliminate the County’s current federal construction authorization status. Federal authorization is an important early step in establishing a potential federal partnership for a beach project, referred to as Shore Protection Project. If the current authorization is forfeited, any future effort to obtain federal participation will likely require new congressional authorization through future WRDA legislation. Reestablishing that authority would take several years, increase uncertainty, and make a future federal partnership more difficult to pursue.
Under authorities provided by the WRDA, the USACE partners with participating local governments to plan and implement Coastal Storm Risk Management (CSRM) projects. These long-term partnerships are intended to address damages from coastal storms, including impacts from erosion to homes, businesses, public infrastructure, and coastal communities through measures such as beach and dune restoration. Project costs are shared between USACE and the participating local government in accordance with applicable federal cost-sharing requirements. Before a project may advance in the WRDA process, it must demonstrate that the anticipated reduction in storm damages and other eligible benefits justify the federal investment, generally through a favorable cost-benefit analysis.
Section 301 of WRDA 2020, as amended by WRDA 2024, directs USACE to identify inactive federal water-resources projects for potential de-authorization when they are no longer considered viable because of a lack of local support, insufficient federal or non-federal resources, or an authorizing purpose that is no longer relevant or feasible. The process is intended to remove projects that are no longer viable while allowing projects that remain relevant and supportable to retain their authorization.
If the Indian River County authorization is preserved and the County later elects to further evaluate a federal partnership, a General Reevaluation Report is typically required to reassess the historic project using current shoreline conditions, engineering data, environmental information, economic criteria, and federal planning requirements. The study would determine whether a modern federal project is technically feasible and economically justified. Any decision to initiate or fund a General Reevaluation Report would return to the Board for separate consideration.
Preserving the authorization would allow staff to continue coordinating with the USACE Jacksonville District regarding the potential scope, costs, benefits, and sponsor obligations associated with a future CSRM project. Federal coastal projects commonly include cost sharing for initial construction and periodic nourishment throughout an authorized program, often 50 years, and may also be eligible for USACE rehabilitation following qualifying storm damage. Eligible local government costs may continue to qualify for funding assistance through the Florida Department of Environmental (FDEP) Protection Beach Management Funding Assistance Program. It is important to note that once a beach project is incorporated into a federal USACE project, it is no longer eligible for assistance through the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance program for the same project area. These funding implications would require further evaluation before any future partnership or cost-sharing agreement is presented to the Board for consideration.
HISTORY
The Indian River County Federal Shore Protection Project dates back to 1980, when the USACE evaluated the County’s Atlantic shoreline and identified areas near Sebastian Inlet and Vero Beach where federal participation could be justified. A favorable Chief of Engineers Report was issued in 1981, and Congress authorized construction through WRDA 1986; however, the project was never constructed. Subsequent design work expanded the Vero Beach segment but identified substantial potential impacts to nearshore hardbottom, and the County did not proceed. Congress reauthorized the project in 1999, and a Limited Reevaluation Report completed in 2000 reduced both the proposed project length and the estimated hardbottom impacts. The project nevertheless did not advance to construction.
The Board of County Commissioners last considered the federal project on June 2, 2015, when the USACE proposed a General Reevaluation Report be completed at an estimated cost of $3 million shared equally between USACE and the County. The study would have updated the project’s engineering, environmental, economic, real estate, and cost analyses and evaluated alternatives intended to reduce impacts to nearshore hardbottom. The Board elected not to enter into the feasibility cost-sharing agreement because of concerns regarding the duration and uncertainty of the federal process, funding obligations, and potential environmental impacts. At that time, the Board was advised that declining to proceed placed the project at risk of future de-authorization.
Following that decision, Staff began preparing a Joint Coastal Permit application for the Sector 5 Beach and Dune Restoration project area in March 2016. FDEP issued the permit in February 2019, and it remains in effect through 2034. Under County-obtained permits, Sector 5 has been constructed twice: first during the winter of 2019–2020 and most recently in March 2026. These projects demonstrate both the continuing need for coastal management and the County’s ongoing commitment to addressing erosion and storm damage.
County staff recently met with representatives of the USACE Jacksonville District to discuss the status of the federal project and available options for preserving the authorization. Jacksonville District staff advised that the County should submit a Letter of Continued Local Support to the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works. The letter would identify the areas the County may wish to evaluate, describe existing coastal damages and risks, and confirm the County’s willingness to continue evaluating a potential cost-sharing agreement for a General Reevaluation Report. This letter would not commit the County to any future actions.
USACE Jacksonville District legal counsel also reviewed the original study authority and determined that it remains sufficient to support a future reevaluation of the existing federal project and other applicable portions of the County’s coastline. Accordingly, no additional congressional study authority would be required at this stage. USACE further advised that initiating a General Reevaluation Report would require federal appropriations through the federal budget, USACE work-plan, or congressional funding process and a financial commitment from the County.
The currently authorized federal project does not match the County’s present Sector 5 Beach and Dune Restoration Project area. The historic federal project was developed using shoreline conditions, economic information, and planning assumptions from the 1980s and 1990s and focused primarily on approximately 1.7 miles of shoreline fronting Vero Beach. By comparison, the County’s current Sector 5 management area extends approximately 3.1 miles and was established independently through the Indian River County Beach Preservation Plan.
Retaining the federal authorization would not automatically convert Sector 5 into a federal project or establish the boundaries of any future federal project. If the County later elects to pursue a General Reevaluation Report, that study would reassess the appropriate project limits using current shoreline conditions, environmental constraints, economic information, public-access requirements, and federal planning criteria. Any proposed changes to the project boundaries or future cost-sharing commitments would be presented to the Board for separate consideration.
title: Preserving the Current Authorization Status of the Indian River County USACE Shore Protection Project

description: On February 4, 2020, the Board adopted Chapter 106 Real Property Disposition Procedures of the Indian River County Code. This section was adopted to allow for an additional method besides the available statutory methods of disposition of county-owned real property. Since that time some issues with the current language of Chapter 106 have arisen. One of those issues is requiring the County to use a real estate broker for the sale or lease of any county-owned property. This includes properties that are currently occupied by tenants who wish to renew their leases with the county as well as people who have approached the county on their own volition to inquire about purchase of certain county parcels. In these last two examples listed it would not only take longer to finalize these transactions but would cost the county more to hire a real estate broker due to the customary 6% fee they charge. These smaller transactions can be negotiated and handled in house by staff, and in doing so would save the county the customary 6% real estate broker fee. The proposed amendments provide requirements to be considered by staff when negotiating a sale or lease. This is to ensure compliance with state statute all while allowing for the saving of taxpayer dollars.
title: Public Hearing for Ordinance Amending Indian River County Code Chapter 106

On March 24th, 2026, members of the nonprofit organization Gifford Community Cultural and Resource Center, Inc. (“GCCRC”) approached the Board and presented a visual depiction of the proposed Project. The Project contemplates preserving the historic church and trails on the site and adding a cultural resource center that includes uses such as a library, studios, classrooms, education, galleries, meeting rooms, play areas, and museum areas. The nonprofit has already met with County planning staff for a Project pre-application meeting and the packet from that meeting is included in this agenda item. In this agenda item, the County Attorney’s office is bringing to the Board for consideration a proposed Resolution and a Lease Agreement between the County and GCCRC for the Property. The Resolution is necessary to comply with Fla. Stat. 125.38, which allows for the sale or lease of property to a nonprofit for a nominal amount, if the Board determines it is in the best interest of the community interest and welfare.
HISTORY OF OWNERSHIP AND DEVELOPMENT OF THE PROPERTY
Although the County began the process to acquire the Property in 1994, the history of the Property spans much further back. The Martin Luther King Jr. Park was known as the Vero Beach Burial Park and later, the Dubose Cemetery, and was acquired in 1929 by the Florida Burial Park, Inc. Later in 1941, the cemetery was transferred to the nonprofit corporation, the Vero Beach Cemetery Association, Inc. Because it was categorized as a nonprofit, the parcel was never on the tax roles and was never sold for taxes when left abandoned. In 1994, the Board of County Commissioners recognized the need to maintain the abandoned cemetery and voted to claim ownership of the Property by pursuing quiet title proceedings. On May 20, 2002, Judge Robert Hawley ordered that title to the Property be vested in the County.
In 1994, after the Board officially voted to pursue ownership of the Property, the Gifford Progressive Civic League led the campaign to save the historic Macedonian Baptist Church, which had been ordered to be demolished or removed from its location in Sebastian, and move it to the Property. The Church was built in 1908, mainly for black railroad workers. In this Lease Agreement, GCCRC proposes to relocate the Church to a different area of the site and incorporate it into the layout of the Project.
In 2001, the Hospital District proposed a lease with the County for a portion of the former cemetery for the construction of the Gifford Health Clinic and the following year, the Board approved for the north 3.5 acres to be rezoned for the project. After the Great Recession in 2008, a walking trail and a playground were added to the remaining Property, which now consists of 5.84 acres.
HISTORIC CEMETERY
There is conflicting information and a difference of opinion among parties whether human remains are still located in the historic cemetery on the Property. Before the Church could be relocated to the Property in 1994, there was some reference in BOCC minutes that a ground penetrating radar survey (GPR) was conducted to confirm if any bodies remain on the Property. We have not been able to find any written report on the conclusions of the GPR, if it was conducted. There are records that indicate bodies were moved to the Crestlawn Cemetery sometime in the 1940s and 1950s. Most recently, in 2013, a GPR was conducted on the Property as part of an environmental site assessment for the development of the Gifford Health Clinic. Phase II of the assessment concluded there was evidence of grave sites, visual observation of headstones, and the presence of subsurface features that could indicate the presence of human remains. The assessment included a map of low, medium, and high probability grave sites. The GCCRC takes the position that those results are ambiguous, since the Property has also historically been a dumping ground for debris.
Although a difference of opinion continues to exist, human remains may exist on the Property. What is certain is that in 1994, the County advertised its intent and informed the state it would maintain the abandoned cemetery and that obligation carries legal responsibilities. If human remains were found during the development of the Project, the legal procedures and rules that apply would depend on whether it is found in a marked or unmarked grave. In its pre-app land use process with Planning staff, GCCRC developed a proposed protocol to be followed if human remains are located during development of the Project. Under the proposed Lease Agreement, if at any phase of testing, excavation, or construction of the Project, suspected human remains are encountered, GCCRC must direct its contractors to immediately cease work so that the County can comply with any applicable state and local regulations regarding the handling of the remains. Before work can restart, the County maintains responsibility for following applicable laws and taking all action necessary to dispose of the human remains and the Lease Agreement assigns GCCRC responsibility for all the costs for site protection, archaeological monitoring, evaluation, reporting, permitting, consultation of agencies, disinterment, and reinternment. It is important to note that this is an issue that the County Attorney and GCCRC were unable to reach an agreement on. GCCRC takes the position that the County should be liable for all these costs and asks that the Board consider this when it acts on this Lease Agreement. To move forward, the parties finally agreed to add language to the paragraph regarding the Tenant’s responsibility for cemetery costs that states, “unless such duties are changed in any future written agreement of the parties.”
title: Consideration of a Lease Agreement for the 5.84 acre Martin Luther King Jr. Park site for the Gifford Cultural Center and Museum ​

description:
Since January 2026, the County has removed three derelict vessels from the Indian River Lagoon, after receiving authorization from Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC).
Derelict vessels are defined by the State of Florida in section 823.11,F.S. as vessels left, stored or abandoned in a wrecked, junked or substantially dismantled condition upon the waters of the state, at a port without the consent of the agency or upon private property without the consent of the owner. Derelict vessels are sinking, degraded, and inoperable, creating navigation hazards, threats to wildlife, and the environment. Vessels designated derelict undergo an extensive investigative process to locate the rightful owner for removal before being submitted to the FWC's Division of Boating and Waterways to approve removal. Natural Resources staff coordinates with FWC to remove approved derelict vessels in a timely manner to reduce risks to the Indian River Lagoon and navigational hazards.
Three additional derelict vessels were recently released by FWC for grant processing and removal. There is one remaining derelict vessel that was investigated and is expected to be removed by FWC.

description:
The Sector 5 project area is a 3.1 mile section of shoreline that extends just north of Tracking Station Beach Park south to just south of the Riomar Golf Course. The Sector 5 project area suffered significant storm related losses to the beach and dune system from the impacts of Hurricanes Ian and Nicole during the 2022 hurricane season. These storm-related impacts, combined with prescribed maintenance activities to address background erosion, created the need for a Sector 5 Hurricanes Ian and Nicole Beach and Dune Restoration Project (Sector 5 Project) to maintain protection of upland properties and infrastructure, while restoring critical habitat for wildlife.
On November 7, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners awarded Bid No. 2025060 to Guettler Brothers Construction, LLC (Guettler), for the Sector 5 Project in the amount of $6,552,025.00 to place approximately 153,300 cubic yards of beach-compatible sand fill and install approximately 117,500 native dune plants. Construction for the Project commenced on November 10, 2025 with substantial completion on March 6, 2026. Approximately 115,901 cubic yards of beach compatible sand was placed along the Sector 5 project area during this time with 117,500 native plants installed along the dune. The contractor (Guettler) completed the Sector 5 Project early, in compliance with permit conditions, and finished under the approved awarded dollar amount for the work.
Change Order No. 1, executed on July 8, 2026, accounts for decreases in contracted amounts of sand delivered/placed in the project area due to changing conditions on the beach throughout the duration of construction. Change Order No. 1 decreases the amount of sand by 37,399 cubic yards (a reduction of $1,308,965.00) and also decreases the Force Account by $689,551.50, resulting in a total net decrease of $1,998,516.50, lowering the completed final project cost to $4,553,508.50.
Construction of the Sector 5 Project has since been deemed complete by the County and contracted Engineer, Aptim Environmental & Infrastructure, LLC (APTIM). On May 19, 2026, the Completion and Certification Statement, a requirement under the permits issued for the Sector 5 Project, was written by APTIM and submitted to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) and the United States Army Corps of Engineers. The dune plants installed were monitored for survival and growth requirements and have successfully passed the 90-day warranty period outlined in the contract.
To date, Guettler has been paid $4,090,163.25, with $215,271.75 held in retainage. Guettler has submitted Contractor’s Application for Payment No. 6 for final payment of work combined with the release of retainage in the total amount of $463,345.25.
Funding for the Sector 5 Project is available through FDEP's Hurricanes Ian and Nicole Recovery Project Grant funds (amended into LGFR 23IR2) and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) obligated federal assistance along with Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM) funding for losses attributed to Hurricanes Ian and Nicole. Funds not covered by the sources identified below will be provided through the Tourist Development Tax.
title: Final Payment and Release of Retainage for Sector 5 Hurricanes Ian and Nicole Beach and Dune Restoration Project

description:
On January 9, 2018, the Board of County Commissioners (BCC) approved a contract with Aptim Environmental and Infrastructure, LLC (APTIM) for professional coastal engineering and biological support services related to the management and nourishment of Sector 3 (Wabasso Beach). The Sector 3 project area is a critically eroded 6.6-mile section of engineered shoreline that extends from the Seaview Subdivision south past the Turtle Trail beach park. The Sector 3 coastline suffered significant storm-related losses to the beach and dune system from the impacts of Hurricanes Ian (2022) and Nicole (2022) creating the need for repair.
On November 7, 2023, the BCC awarded Bid No. 2024004 to Dickerson Infrastructure, Inc. dba Dickerson Florida, Inc. for the Sector 3 Hurricanes Ian and Nicole Dune Renourishment Project. Construction commenced on December 1, 2023, and completed on April 13, 2024. The project consisted of a dune restoration project that placed approximately 223,040 cubic yards of beach compatible sand fill and installed 728,633 native dune plants along the shoreline in Indian River County from Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) range monuments R20 to R55.
Regulatory permits issued for the beach restoration activities identify post-construction related monitoring to be performed on a set schedule for several years following completion of construction. These monitoring activities are evaluated to demonstrate compliance with permit conditions.
Proposed APTIM Work Order No. 2018006-22, in the amount of $28,338.00 provides professional services for assessing the project performance in the form of a Year 2 Physical Monitoring Report related to the Sector 3 Hurricanes Ian and Nicole Dune Renourishment Project. APTIM deliverables under Work Order 2018006-22 are expected to be submitted to the County within 90 days of the County's 2026 summer hydrographic survey data being provided to APTIM.
All subsequent post-construction required monitoring of the Sector 3 Hurricanes Ian and Nicole Dune Renourishment Project will be addressed through future work orders.
title: Work Order No. 2018006-22-APTIM, Sector 3 Hurricanes Ian and Nicole Dune Renourishment Year 2 Physical Monitoring Report

On January 1, 2026, the County issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) inviting not-for-profit and for-profit organizations, government agencies, and individuals to apply for funding to support children’s programs and services in Indian River County. This grant program is administered by Indian River County with assistance from the Children’s Services Advisory Committee (CSAC), consistent with Ordinance Number 2022-007 and the County’s Outside Agency Funding Policy Revisions approved by the Board on August 4, 2022. In response to the RFP, the County received 50 proposals requesting a total of $3,957,041 in funding. The funding dashboard for all 50 proposals is on the Children Service’s Website.
Over the past 10 months, staff have collaborated with the CSAC Main Committee, the Needs Assessment Subcommittee, and the Grants Subcommittee to refine the RFP process. The goal is to ensure the needs of the children and families in our community are met, to provide agencies with professional development and coaching to develop strong RFPs, to establish clear measurable outcomes for agencies, to analyze and share impact reports with the public, and to increase transparency throughout the process. Below is a timeline of the work that has been done to improve the RFP process by enhancing accountability and impact.

description: Indian River County originally initiated this case in 2018 to affirm the public’s right to use the beach in Summerplace for customary recreational uses. At the time, there was a new Florida statute in place (Fla. 163.035) that established the process for local governments to pursue customary use designations. Ultimately, the Court decided that the County did not correctly follow the prescribed statutory procedures and the County lost the case. During that litigation, a neighbor, Mr. Robert M. Jaffee, filed a counterclaim against the County alleging it breached the terms of a 2009 temporary beach renourishment easement when it filed the customary use lawsuit. The Court ruled in Jaffee’s favor and awarded him $1.00 in damages. Despite this low verdict, Jaffee was entitled to his costs. The County has already settled Mr. Jaffee’s claim for costs for $2500 in 2025. However, during the litigation, Mr. Jaffee also filed four motions for attorneys’ fees based upon Fla. Stat. 57.105, alleging that the County’s decision to file the original suit was frivolous and that the County engaged in other litigation misconduct. A trial was scheduled for July 10, 2026, for the Court to hear the evidence and rule on Jaffee’s motions. The County is represented by Paul Berg, Esq in this case. Although the County is confident that Mr. Jaffee’s motions are meritless, to avoid the continued costs of litigating this matter, the County Attorney made Mr. Jaffee a $25,000 offer to fully settle all his motions and claims contingent on Board of County Commissioner approval. The trial has been postponed while the parties attempt to settle this matter.
title: Approval of the Settlement Agreement for IRC v. Twenty-Two Beachfront Properties et. al

attachments.name: Indian River County Agreement with Thrive for Juvenile Diversion Programs

description:
Pursuant to Section 939.185, Florida Statutes, the Indian River County (County) collects fees specifically for the operation and administration of juvenile alternative programs. Historically, the local juvenile diversion program has been administered by the Court Administration for the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit (Court Administration).
On April 9, 2018, Chief Judge Metzger of the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit wrote a letter to the County which indicated the Court Administration would no longer administer the juvenile diversion programs after July 31, 2018.
On May 14, 2018, the Florida Department of Juvenile Justice (DJJ) sent a letter to the County stating that it intends to partner with agencies in the community to ensure that the local youth receive civil citations and/or diversion opportunities. To do so, however, DJJ would need the remaining funds collected pursuant to Section 939.185, Florida Statutes, for current fiscal year 2017/2018.
On July 3, 2018, the Indian River Board of County Commissioners (Board) approved the recommendation by the County's Director of the Office of Management and Budget to authorize DJJ to assume responsibility for the administration of the local juvenile diversion program. The Board directed the County Attorney's Office to develop an interlocal agreement between the County and the DJJ for the Chairman's signature.
On December 18, 2018, the Indian River Board of County Commissioners approved the Interlocal Agreement between Indian River County and the State of Florida Department of Juvenile Justice. Under this agreement, the County agreed to provide funds on an annual basis to DJJ to provide juvenile diversion programs (civil citation or other diversion programs) for Indian River County. DJJ agreed to receive funds annually for distribution. For FY 2019, the County agreed to pay $27,500 for juvenile diversion programs. For FY 2020 and thereafter, the County agreed to remit to DJJ a portion of the fees collected annually pursuant to Section 939.185, Florida Statutes. DJJ invoiced the County in October of each fiscal year for services provided during the previous fiscal year.
DJJ contracted with Thrive, Inc to provide juvenile diversion programs (civil citation or other diversion programs) for Indian River County. DJJ distributed funding for services to Thrive, Inc. upon documentation of services delivered to Indian River County youth. Services include assessment of service needs; Individual Service Plan; Case Management; Restitution Collection; Community Service Oversight; Delinquency Interventions and/or Mental Health or Substance Abuse services.
DJJ was required to provide an annual report on the results of the program operation. The report contained the following information: number of youth admitted in the fiscal year, number of youth who completed the program in the fiscal year, and number of youth who offended during services in the fiscal year.
title: Agreement Between Indian River County and Thrive, Inc to Provide Juvenile Diversion Programs

description:
Many of the key pieces of equipment utilized throughout the County are specialized due to facility design, and/or are standardized for consistency of operations, especially at Utilities treatment facilities. These items have been designated as sole source, indicating they are only available directly from the manufacturer, or from the manufacturer’s lone authorized distributor for our area.
A sole source designation provides Procurement staff the authority to issue Purchase Orders as soon after the need for the goods or services is identified, after appropriate review and approval of a requisition, and ensures the expenditures for each item or vendor are appropriately authorized ahead of time.
Board sole source designations are considered valid for three years, and supporting documentation is verified at each renewal or addition.
title: Sole Source Procurement Designation Renewals

description:
Bridge No. 884019 carries CR-505 (Roseland Road) over Collier Creek (a tributary to the Sebastian River Prong) in northern Indian River County. The existing bridge consists of a timber pile-supported structure with block abutments that has been in service since 1958 with last full restoration completed in 1992.
Routine bridge inspections performed in accordance with the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Bridge Inspection Program have identified continued deterioration of the structure. Based on the condition of the bridge and anticipated repair needs, replacement of the structure has been determined to be the most practical long-term solution.
The proposed project will replace the existing bridge with a new structure designed to meet current applicable design standards while maintaining this important transportation connection. To expedite project delivery, the County is procuring surveying and geotechnical services under separate agreements. In addition, the County has obtained a St. Johns River Water Management District Environmental Resource Permit Exemption.
title: Work Order No. 02, Consor North America, Inc. CR-505/Roseland Road over Collier Creek, Tributary to Sebastian River Prong, Bridge No. 884019 (IRC-2519)

description:
On behalf of the Parks Division, sealed bids were solicited for construction of the Hobart Ballfield project, which includes the conversion of the existing adult multipurpose field into a college-regulation baseball field; upgrades to an existing softball/little league field; construction of a new softball/hybrid field; lighting improvements; a scoreboard; stormwater improvements; a pump station; parking lot and pathway improvements; landscaping; and construction of a concession/restroom building. The project was designed by Masteller & Moler, Inc.
On April 8, 2025, the Board awarded bid 2025030 to Proctor Construction Company, LLC (“Proctor”) for Hobart Park Baseball Field Improvements, based on designs prepared by Masteller & Moler, Inc. On the design plans, the existing softball field was shown with no improvements to be made besides sidewalks leading to the field, and it was labeled “Existing Field To Remain.” The design also omitted any presence of batting cages on this property, which prior to construction, was the site of four lanes of batting cages that were donated to the County and were frequently utilized. These batting cages were removed from the site by the County as construction began.
The third field has not been significantly upgraded in the last ten years, and many existing amenities are in disrepair. Based on the existing condition of the third field, there are multiple items that are needed in order to bring this field to an acceptable playing standard. These items include: (#1) fencing and backstop replacement; (#2) replacing the existing Bahia grass with Bermuda sod; (#3) Extending the new irrigation system to this field from the newly installed fields; (#4) Replacing the aged, wooden dugouts with new ones; and (#5) Adding new batting cages to the complex.
title: Hobart Ballfield Project — Change Order #2 — Construction Bond and Builders Risk Policy Increase
