attachments.name: IRC Business Impact Estimate - Housing Trust Fund - DRAFT v2

description:
It is requested that the data herein presented be given formal consideration by the Board of County Commissioners at its regular meeting of August 4, 2026.
In line with the Indian River County Comprehensive Plan Evaluation and Appraisal Report (EAR) requirement for affordable/workforce housing to be made available, the Community Services Department initiated the establishment of an Attainable Housing Trust Fund (“Trust”). The Trust is structured as a land acquisition, land banking, and for-profit, and nonprofit disposition program. It is designed to advance the County’s attainable housing objectives while minimizing operational and financial risk.
Properties will be acquired by the Trust through various methods, including, but not limited to:
• Voluntary developer contributions
• Foreclosure
• Code enforcement
• Board-designated proceeds from the sale or disposition of County-owned property
• Grants, donations, inter local contributions, and other lawful sources
• Interest earnings on Trust balances
• Private philanthropy donations
Properties may be vacant or have structures that require rehabilitation to become suitable for habitation.
Permitted uses for the Trust:
• Land acquisition and land banking.
• Property conveyance to for-profit and nonprofit organizations.
• Administrative costs for program administration are capped at 10% of the total available funds in the Trust account.
Governance Structure:
• Board of County Commissioners – Will have the final authority.
• Affordable Housing Advisory Committee (AHAC) – Will play an advisory role.
• Community Services Department SHIP Administrator – Will be responsible for program management.
• Planning and Development – Will be responsible for review and assessment of properties to be acquired.
• County Attorney – Will provide legal oversight and compliance.
• Finance Department – Will provide financial oversight and compliance.
Disposition Process:
County Attorney’s Office
• Verify title status
• Draft acquisition and conveyance language
Planning and Development Department
• Evaluate location, zoning and infrastructure viability
• Assess development feasibility
County Attorney’s Office
• Secure BOCC authorization to purchase or accept property
•Record county ownership
Planning and Development Department
• Classify property as surplus and designate for attainable housing
Community Services - SHIP Administrator
• Develop and publish RFQ to create a register of development partners (for profit and nonprofit organizations).
AHAC
• Review RFQ and make recommendations of eligible development partners to the BOCC
BOCC
• Approves eligible development partners to be added to register
AHAC
• Offers available properties to partners on register in order of ranking by highest scoring agency
Procurement and SHIP Administrator
• Execute conveyance agreements
• Record conveyance documents
title: SHIP — Consideration of the Indian River ​County Attainable Housing Trust Ordinance

description:
On August 19, 2025, the Board approved the Rain Tree Corner Subdivision POA’s request to establish a special assessment in the amount of $300,000, based upon a quote of $286,745 provided by the POA, to fund the replacement of the culvert on the sole access road for their 16-home subdivision, located at the intersection of 12th Street and 54th Avenue.
The Board awarded Bid 2025058 for As Needed Culvert Replacement and Repair to three contractors. On October 7, 2025, the Board approved staff to proceed with the replacement of the Rain Tree Corners culvert for a potential cost of $250,000 based upon quotes received from County contractors.
The Board approved the Initial Assessment Resolution on April 7, 2026. Subsequently, the contractor filed a significant change order due to a material condition change upon the initiation of work. The change order increased the cost due to more stringent requirements of Indian River Farms Water District. Additionally, some language was inadvertently left out of the initial resolution relating to interest payments. Public Works negotiated with the contractor in an effort to bring the total price down to a level commensurate with the August 2025 proposal. The total project price is estimated to be between $330,000 and $350,000. Upon further design review, Public Works has determined that the project will assist with the longevity and maintenance of 12th Street in the area of 54th Avenue due to the upgraded design and character of the new pipe. The roadway will last longer and, as such, lead to long-term asset protection. Therefore, the Board passed an Amended Initial Resolution on June 16, 2026, in which the property owners will pay the portion of the project that specially benefits their properties in the estimated amount of $300,000 and the County will fund any amount over and above that amount due to design enhancements to the roadway.
title: Final Assessment Resolution for Rain Tree Corner Subdivision Culvert Replacement Project

description:
MBV Engineering, Inc., has applied on behalf of Westside Racquet Club LLC, to expand an existing racquet club facility located at 4291 5th Place SW that will be improved in four phases. The special exception use request will cover all four phases. However, only Phase 1 is included in this site plan approval request, and each subsequent phase will require a separate site plan review and approval in the future. The site is located east of 43rd Avenue, north of 6th Lane SW, and South of 5th Place SW (see attachment 1). The site is zoned RS-3, Single-Family Residential (up to 3 units per acre). Special exception use approval is required to expand the existing racquet club facility.
The subject site is improved with a 2,390 square foot (SF) building that is used as a clubhouse and eight (8) tennis courts. All existing improvements are proposed to remain, with the intent of restoring the current facilities and incorporating additional enhancements. Phase I includes the restoration of the existing eight (8) tennis courts, construction of four (4) new padel courts, and associated site improvements (i.e. utilities, stormwater, parking, and landscaping). Phase II consists of restoring the existing 2,390 SF clubhouse building and the construction of two (2) additional padel courts. Phase III proposes the addition of a pool as a clubhouse amenity, and the construction of four (4) pickleball courts. Phase IV includes the construction of two (2) additional tennis courts.
The Board of County Commissioners (BCC) is to consider the special exception use and site plan approval (Phase 1 only), conduct a public hearing, and vote to approve, approve with conditions, or deny the request for special exception use. Pursuant to Section 971.05 of the County land development regulations (LDRs), the BCC is to consider the appropriateness of the requested use for the subject site and compatibility of the use with the surrounding area. The BCC may recommend reasonable conditions and safeguards necessary to mitigate impacts and ensure compatibility of the use with the surrounding area.
title: Westside Racquet Club LLC’s Request for Special Exception Use and Site Plan Approval to Construct and Operate a Racquet Club Facility [SP-SE-25-05-17 / 91060129-97640] (Quasi-Judicial)

description:
The subject properties, comprising approximately ± 10.4 acres, are located on the East side of U.S. Highway 1, South of and adjacent to 61st Street. The properties are split-zoned with RM-3, Multiple-Family Residential District fronting U.S. 1 on the west side of the parcels, and RS-3, Single-Family Residential District on the East side of the parcels (Attachment 1). They are located within the Urban Service Area (USA) and have a Future Land Use designation of L-1, Low-Density Residential-1 (up to 3 units/acre) (Attachment 2).
The applicant’s justification letter states, “The project is to develop an assisted living and memory care facility on 14.94 acres. Currently, the property has split zoning between RS-3 and RM-3. The request is to rezone the property completely to RM-3 zoning to make the full economic use and benefit of the property, as well as continue harmonious development patterns and avoid unintended consequences of a single parcel of land being developed using two different zonings. The application further requests to rezone additional parcels south of the subject property to remedy the split zoning problem that encumbers properties between 61st and 57th streets. The result of the rezonings will achieve conformance with the Indian River County's Comprehensive Plan and support logical development patterns along U.S. Highway 1.”
The area is currently undeveloped; therefore, the proposed rezoning would establish a unified zoning district before development occurs, allowing the parcels to be reviewed and developed more cohesively under one set of zoning standards. The request does not increase the maximum residential density but instead aligns the zoning with the Future Land Use designation and does indeed support a more logical development pattern along the U.S. Highway 1 corridor.
Existing Land Use Pattern
The surrounding area is largely undeveloped; therefore, the existing land use pattern is best understood through the area’s zoning history and current zoning configuration described below. The subject properties have been affected by split zoning since the original 1975–1985 Indian River County Zoning Atlas, which placed commercial zoning along the U.S. Highway 1 frontage and RS-3 zoning on the eastern portion of the parcels (Attachment 3). In 1985, the County converted the former C-1A zoning within the residential future land use area to RM-3, through Ordinance 86-15 (Attachment 4), while the eastern portions of the parcels remained zoned RS-3.
To the north, across 61st Street, which is an unpaved roadway with an existing canal, properties remain similarly undeveloped and split-zoned RM-3 and RS-3. To the east of the subject properties is the Spoonbill Preserve Planned Development, approved by Ordinance 2019-005, which rezoned approximately 413.67 acres from RS-3 and CON-2, Estuarine Wetlands Conservation District to PD, Planned Development. That rezoning established a large, planned development area extending east toward the Indian River Lagoon, leaving the RS-3 zoning on the eastern portions of the subject parcels as a remnant of the prior zoning pattern. To the south, the adjacent properties along U.S. Highway 1 contain the same RM-3/RS-3 split-zoning pattern and are developed with existing single-family residences. However, those properties were not included in this rezoning request because the property owners did not authorize their inclusion and the RS-3 district ultimately corners off along the PD district. Across U.S. Highway 1 to the west is an established Commercial/Industrial node containing properties zoned IL, Light Industrial.
Since the subject area has not yet developed, the requested rezoning would resolve the existing split-zoning condition before development occurs. Rezoning the subject properties entirely to RM-3 would place each parcel under one zoning district, allow for more cohesive site planning, and better align the zoning pattern with the applicable Future Land Use designation. The request does not represent a change to an established development pattern, but rather a cleanup of historical zoning boundaries to support logical future development along the U.S. Highway 1 corridor.
Zoning District Differences
In terms of allowed uses, there are both similarities and differences between the RS-3 and RM-3 zoning districts (Attachment 5). The distinctions between these two zoning districts are best illustrated through their respective purpose statements. These purpose statements provide a clear framework for understanding the intent and scope of each district's allowable uses and development potential. The purpose statements are as follows:
RS-3: Single-Family Residential District (up to 3 units/acre): The RS-3 districts are established to implement the policies of the Indian River County Comprehensive Plan for managing land designated for residential uses, providing single-family housing opportunities, and ensuring adequate public facilities. These districts are also intended to implement the county's housing policies by providing opportunities for a varied and diverse housing supply.
RM-3: Multiple-Family Residential District (up to 3 units/acre): The RM-3 districts are established to implement the policies of the Indian River County Comprehensive Plan for managing land designated for residential uses, providing opportunities for multifamily residential units and ensuring adequate public facilities to meet the needs of residents. These districts are also intended to implement the county's housing policies by providing opportunities for a varied and diverse housing supply.
title: Valerie Balfe and William Wagner's Request to Rezone Approximately 10.4 Acres from RS-3, Single-Family Residential District to RM-3, Multiple-Family Residential District [2023-03-0038 / 99067] [Quasi-Judicial]

description:
Pioneering Change, Inc., a local nonprofit organization, has requested that the Board of County Commissioners support the attached resolution to designate the Gifford community as a Florida Children’s Initiative (“FCI”). Fla. Stat. Section 409.147 establishes a process for a county or municipality to apply to the State of Florida Ounce of Prevention Fund of Florida, Inc. for the FCI designation. According to the statute, the purpose of the designation is for the state to identify severely disadvantaged areas and provide guidance and resources to assist communities to address critical needs.
Both the statute and the attached Florida Children’s Initiative Overview & Designation Process that is available on the Ounce of Prevention website state that it must be a county or municipality that applies for the FCI designation. Page 5 of the Florida Children’s Initiative Overview & Designation Process details all the information that a municipality or county must submit to the Ounce of Prevention Fund for consideration. It is unclear in either the statute or this overview what the deadline is for submitting the application. However, Pioneering Change Inc. has engaged in a planning process and informed the Board at its June 16, 2026, meeting that there is a June 30th deadline.

description:
Indian River County (County) is located on Florida’s East Coast, which is adjacent to the Atlantic Ocean. This creates a high level of vulnerability for the County to sustain major hurricane impacts. Hurricanes can create catastrophic wind damage, storm surge, and flooding damage, which may delay the arrival of emergency (mass care) supplies. In part, emergency supplies may include food, water, tarps, and other essential supplies during the early stages of a post-disaster response for our communities.
Indian River County Emergency Management (IRC EM) has the capability to make pre-landfall resource requests to the Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM) when a Declaration of Emergency has been made. Such resources require local storage locations during a hurricane event. IRC EM has collaborated with the School District of Indian River County (SDIRC) to form an Interlocal Agreement (Exhibit 1 - Attached), which would allow the pre-staging and temporary storage of emergency supplies in SDIRC facilities should an emergency or disaster threaten our community. The pre-stage emergency supplies can then be disseminated immediately after roadways are cleared of debris, flooding, or other hazards.
title: Approval of Temporary Emergency Supply Storage Interlocal Agreement

description:
The Indian River County Department of Utility Services (IRCDUS) currently utilizes a legacy Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS) to support maintenance management activities across the utility system. As IRCDUS’s operational, maintenance, and asset management programs have evolved, IRCDUS identified the need for a modern enterprise CMMS platform capable of supporting mobile field operations, integrated asset management workflows, improved data governance, and long-term infrastructure lifecycle management.
IRCDUS operates a complex utility system consisting of water distribution systems, wastewater collection systems, treatment facilities, lift stations, and associated mechanical, electrical, instrumentation, and process assets. The Department also maintains multiple enterprise systems, including GIS, customer information system (CIS), supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system, inspection platforms, and operational databases which require integration with the CMMS environment.
To support these operational objectives, the County issued Request for Proposals (RFP) #2026016 for a CMMS software platform and associated implementation services. The requested solution included management of both horizontal and vertical utility assets, mobile and offline field functionality, configurable asset hierarchy structures, integration with existing enterprise systems, workflow management and preventive maintenance capabilities, data migration services, training and change management support, and phased implementation services focused on long-term operational adoption.
Eleven (11) proposals were submitted, determined to be initially responsive, and presented for review. A selection committee was designated and approved by the County Administrator, with each committee member independently reviewing and scoring the proposals in accordance with the criteria established in the RFP. The committee met and established an overall ranking of firms. The five top ranked firms were invited to participate in demonstrations, after which the committee independently ranked the firms in order of preference. The two top ranked firms were invited to participate in in-person demonstrations with the committee and end users. Following the in-person demonstrations, the committee again independently ranked the firms, and declared the ranking final, with MentorAPM the highest ranked and recommended firm. MentorAPM demonstrated utility-focused experience, implementation methodology, integration capabilities, mobile functionality, operational alignment, and phased deployment approach.
title: Award of RFP #2026016 – Computerized Maintenance Management System Software and Implementation Services, IRCDUS Project ID: 00.23.541

description:
The owner of the property (hereinafter “developer”) located at 7625 9th Street SW, Vero Beach, FL 32968. The developer was required to provide certain improvements along with its development. One of those required improvements is that of utilities infrastructure on their property and on county property. The county is receiving an easement for the area over their property on which the newly constructed utilities infrastructure is located. There will also be a bill of sale for all the utility infrastructure that the developer will be purchasing and installing on both their property and county property, this way the infrastructure is officially owned by the County.
Under the normal process, this is done pursuant to an easement and bill of sale with a 1-year warranty on the work performed by the developer via a security instrument such as a bond or letter of credit. Also, should the property that the utility easement and infrastructure are located on be encumbered by a mortgage, a consent and joinder to the utility easement and infrastructure is required to be obtained from the mortgage company. In this case, the mortgage company will only agree to sign off on the consent and joinder with the additional rider to the easement and bill of sale that is attached hereto. The County Attorney’s Office has worked alongside utilities to bring the attached rider to the easement and bill of sale to an acceptable state that would not leave the county unprotected. As this rider to the easement and bill of sale is a separate contractual document, it requires approval from the Board as there is no authority for staff to bind the County for this particular reason. For this reason, staff, after review of the attached rider, is bringing this item to the Board to receive approval of the rider agreement by the Board and subsequent execution by the Chair.

description:
On August 19, 2025, the Board approved the Rain Tree Corner Subdivision POA’s request to establish a special assessment in the amount of $300,000, based upon a quote of $286,745 provided by the POA, to fund the replacement of the culvert on the sole access road for their 16-home subdivision, located at the intersection of 12th Street and 54th Avenue.
The Board awarded Bid 2025058 for As Needed Culvert Replacement and Repair to three contractors. On October 7, 2025, the Board approved staff to proceed with the replacement of the Rain Tree Corners culvert for a potential cost of $250,000 based upon quotes received from County contractors.
The Board approved the Initial Assessment Resolution on April 7, 2026. Subsequently, the contractor filed a significant change order due to a material condition change upon the initiation of work. The change order increased the cost due to more stringent requirements of Indian River Farms Water District. Additionally, some language was inadvertently left out of the initial resolution relating to interest payments. Public Works negotiated with the contractor in an effort to bring the total price down to a level commensurate with the August 2025 proposal. The total project price is estimated to be between $330,000 and $350,000. Upon further design review, Public Works has determined that the project will assist with the longevity and maintenance of 12th Street in the area of 54th Avenue due to the upgraded design and character of the new pipe. The roadway will last longer and, as such, lead to long-term asset protection. Therefore, the property owners will pay the portion of the project that specially benefits their properties in the estimated amount of $300,000 and the County will fund any amount over and above that amount due to design enhancements to the roadway.
title: Amended Initial Assessment Resolution for Rain Tree Corner Subdivision Culvert Replacement Project

description:
Part II of Chapter 204 of the Indian River County Code of Ordinances was adopted in 1994 to establish the Solid Waste Disposal District (SWDD) and to provide procedures for levying and collecting special assessments to fund solid waste disposal services within Indian River County.
In 2025, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 2025-10, creating Chapter 206 of the County Code, entitled the Master Capital and Service Assessment Ordinance. Chapter 206 establishes a uniform process for the levy, collection, and administration of special assessments for both capital improvements and essential public services in accordance with Section 197.3632, Florida Statutes.
The proposed ordinance updates Part II of Chapter 204 to align the Solid Waste Disposal District assessment process with the procedures established in Chapter 206. The amendments eliminate duplicative procedural provisions that are now addressed through the County’s master assessment framework and clarify certain definitions related to solid waste management.
Attached to this item is the proposed ordinance, the required Business Impact Estimate, and the existing language of Part II of Chapter 204 for context.

description:
On May 6, 2025, the Board approved an Area of Operation Resolution authorizing the St. Lucie County Housing Finance Authority (HFA), and independent agency, to exercise its authority within Indian River County for the purpose of financing the Orchard Grove Apartments project. On May 15, 2025, the St. Lucie County HFA approved the issuance of up to $28,000,000 in Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds on behalf of Vero Beach Leased Housing Associates IV, LLLP for the Orchard Grove Apartments project.
Under Section 147(f) of the Internal Revenue Code, commonly referred to as the TEFRA process, tax-exempt private activity bonds cannot be issued unless notice is provided to the public, a public hearing is conducted, and approval is granted by the applicable elected officials of the jurisdiction where the project is located. The Board conducted the original TEFRA hearing for this project on June 6, 2025.
The St. Lucie County HFA did not initially have sufficient 2025 bond volume allocation available for the Orchard Grove project. However, on January 2, 2026, the HFA obtained a 2026 project-specific bond allocation for Orchard Grove. In addition, the HFA held unused 2025 carryforward bond allocation from another project. Under federal tax law, previously carried forward bond allocation must be used before current-year allocation can be applied. At the same time, Florida law requires current-year bond allocation to be used only for the specific project for which it was awarded.
The project that had priority use of the 2025 carryforward allocation did not close until late March 2026. As a result, Orchard Grove’s financing could not proceed before the original TEFRA approvals expired. Federal tax regulations require the bonds to be issued within 12 months of the Board’s approval.
Because the prior approvals expired before the financing could close, Orchard Grove is now required to obtain new TEFRA approvals from both St. Lucie County and Indian River County in order to proceed with the bond issuance.
The St. Lucie County Housing Finance Authority will be holding a new TEFRA hearing and asked to approve a final Authorizing Resolution to finalize the sale of the bonds in the near future.
The proposed bonds are limited obligations payable solely from revenues generated by the project. Indian River County will not be responsible for repayment of the bonds and will have no financial liability or obligation associated with the financing.
title: St. Lucie County Housing Finance Authority Bonds Hearing - Orchard Grove - TEFRA

description:
On June 3, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners approved the County’s group insurance program for the plan year October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026. During this meeting there was discussion regarding projected plan performance and the potential impact of the increased cost related to GLP-1 for weight loss. It was noted that under the new pharmacy PBM, Rightway, GLP-1 weight loss medications would require prior authorization criteria for BMI and co-morbidity to be met in order to be covered under the plan. Additionally, months earlier the Trump Administration announced its Rx Plan, of which one of the medications to be impacted was GLP-1's. Thus, Admininstration advised we continue and see what rolled out from the President's Rx Plan.
Ultimately, there were no changes made to the group health plan, there were no increases in group health plan premiums, and it was determined staff would continue to monitor plan financials and report back to the Board. Since that time, plan experience under our current plan year has reflected a substantial increase in medical high-cost claims as well as a continued increase in GLP-1 weight loss medications (and costs), necessitating the Board to consider modifications to the plan as well as make necessary premium increases to fund the plan benefits.
Staff met with the Board on March 24, May 5, and May 19, 2026, to discuss group insurance plan performance and provided recommendations for funding requirements, plan modifications, and premium amounts for the upcoming plan year beginning October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027.
Following the May 19, 2026, BOCC meeting, staff scheduled four (4) Microsoft Teams meetings to review proposed changes with employees and retirees on May 29th and June 5th. Informational notices were delivered to work sites for all covered employees and emailed or mailed to retirees with general information and encouraging members to participate in the Microsoft Teams meetings. Information was also provided to each of the constitutional agencies. Additionally, a recording of the May 29th Microsoft Team’s meeting was placed on the HR Staff Portal to provide access to individuals who could not attend one of the 4 informational sessions. Individuals had the opportunity to ask questions and an FAQ was prepared and posted on the HR Staff Portal and shared with County Administration.
title: Group Health Insurance Plan Funding, Plan Design, and Premiums for FY26/27

description:
This item requests authorization for staff to prepare a site-specific resolution and interlocal agreement for the Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) Program, for a new business and property owner located in unincorporated Indian River County, at 9055 17th Place, Vero Beach, FL.
On May 8, 2026, the Indian River County Economic Development Team of County Staff and the Indian River County Chamber, received a request from a new business, to utilize the Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) Program, for its planned facility located at 9055 17th Place. The C-PACE Program is authorized pursuant to §163.08, Florida Statutes, provided that the local government adopts a resolution authorizing a program administrator to manage the program within its jurisdiction.
The new business, ParadICE, LLC is renovating the property suitable for manufacturing of commercial ice products sold wholesale to large retailers. In addition, the company plans to produce specialty cocktail ice products for restaurants and hospitality customers. ParadICE, LLC is also the property owner at the location of this proposed new business.
The owners of the company have engaged the Florida Development Finance Corporation (FDFC) to assist them with C-PACE financing. FDFC is a nonprofit statewide conduit issuer of taxable and tax-exempt bonds, formed under §288.9603, Florida Statutes. FDFC is partnered with the Florida Resiliency Energy District (FRED), which serves as the program administrator for the C-PACE Program. FDFC will perform the underwriting for the proposed financing, and FRED will administer the program for ParadICE, LLC.
Indian River County has not adopted a countywide authorization for the C-PACE Program; however, in 2022, the Board of County Commissioners approved a site-specific resolution and an interlocal agreement with a project administrator, authorizing a business located at 5380 U.S. Highway 1 to utilize the C-PACE Program. Thereby, ParadICE, LLC is seeking a similar site-specific approval to participate in the C-PACE Program.
title: Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) Program Consideration for 9055 17th Place

description:
On March 8, 2022, the County Administrator provided the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners (“BCC”) with a proposed resolution authorizing an Environmental Land Bond Referendum for the November 8, 2022, ballot. Resolution 2022-016 was passed by majority vote. The Resolution calls for a Bond Referendum Election for the issuance of general obligation bonds as follows: “To acquire and permanently preserve environmentally significant lands to restore the Indian River Lagoon, protect water resources, natural areas, wildlife habitat, drinking water resources, and construct public access improvements related thereto, shall Indian River County be authorized to issue general obligation bonds up to $50,000,000, maturing within 20 years from each issuance, not exceeding the legal maximum interest rate, payable from ad valorem taxes, with full public disclosure of all spending through annual independent audits.”
The BCC established the Environmental Land Acquisition Panel (ELAP) as a nine-member group to review information provided during the application process and provide recommendations to the BCC regarding the prioritization of the acquisition of environmentally sensitive lands. The ELAP has held twenty meetings between August 2023 and September 2025.
The County’s environmental bond process allows the public to nominate properties for acquisition at any time during the year. Each nomination period is six months, at which time that period closes and nominated properties are ranked by the ELAP. The close of the first ranking period was on August 31, 2024. Throughout the process, staff and consultants have reached out to landowners to determine which parcels had owners wanting to have their property considered for acquisition through the environmental bond process (“willing sellers”). Owners of parcels nominated by the public were contacted via letter, email and telephone to determine whether the owner was a willing seller. The initial nomination period identified twenty-three nominations with willing sellers. Of these twenty-three nominations, sixteen nominations were submitted as
“fee simple” nominations (County purchases the property outright), and seven were nominated as potential conservation easements.
On January 14, 2025, the ELAP met to rank the nominated properties. Following the ELAP ranking, the properties were “Tiered” to prioritize the process of negotiations with landowners. On March 11, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners approved the ELAP Final Ranking and Tiered List of Nominations. At this meeting, the Board authorized staff to pursue Tier 1 Ranked Properties for acquisition consistent with the ELAP’s recommendation, including the authority to make conditional offers of purchase and sale subject to approval by the Board of County Commissioners, and in accordance with Florida Statute Section 125.355.
At the March 11, 2025, BCC meeting, the Board authorized staff to move forward with the next steps in the land acquisition process, which include obtaining two independent appraisals for the subject property, and to undertake purchase negotiations with the landowner based on these appraisals.
12300-Archie Carr is a Board approved Tier 1 property. The 9.7-acre property is a singular parcel located on Highway A1A, and is located half of a mile north of Pelican Island National Wildlife Refuge and two miles south of Sebastian Inlet State Park. The site includes a fifty (50) year old single-family residence in poor condition. The environmental conditions on the property are detailed in the report prepared by Water & Air Research, Inc. which is included as Attachment 1.
The following summarizes the parcel information for the 12300-Archie Carr property.

The proposed use of the property would be for environmental conservation and passive public recreation. The property has 2.3 acres of oceanfront uplands and 6.73 acres of submerged land located across Highway A1A in the Indian River Lagoon. The eastern (beachfront) portion of the property is within the Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge. Staff have been notified that this parcel is eligible for cost-share funding through the Deepwater Horizon monies used for acquisition and restoration of property within the Refuge. Additionally, if acquired, staff will be pursuing cost-share funding for this property through the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program which provides funding towards the purchase of properties having the potential for claims resulting from extreme environmental events.
Because the property is valued at more than $500,000, the County's Environmental Lagoon Program Guide and the State statutes require that two independent appraisals be obtained to determine an “approved appraised value” for the property. Staff obtained appraisals from Tuttle, Armfield & Wagner Appraisal Research, Inc. (TAW) and Clayton, Roper & Marshall (CRM). The appraisals completed by TAW and B&D are included as Attachment 2. The Assistant County Attorney and the County’s Land Acquisition & Lease Specialist coordinated with the landowners’ realtor, and a sale price was negotiated. The owners have executed a contract for sale in the amount of $5,500,000.00 (Attachment 3).

description:
On July 16, 2019, the Solid Waste Disposal District (SWDD) and Indian River Eco District, LLC entered into a Landfill Gas Agreement for the refinement of the gases produced at the landfill into renewable natural gas. The Agreement has been assigned to Nopetro Eco District LLC (NED), a Florida limited liability company, and has had four amendments, the most recent being heard by the Board on January 23, 2024.
Section 3.3C of the 3rd Amendment includes provision for Commercial and Environmental Improvement (CEI) projects that may be proposed by NED and that SWDD may elect to jointly fund but have no obligation to do so. The section does require NED to issue a notice to SWDD of the terms of the agreement for the CEI project to include respective responsibilities for such improvements. On May 31, 2026, NED has provided the attached letter with a notice to proceed with CEI project to include landfill gas improvements to help increase the quantity and quality of landfill gas for the Renewable Natural Gas (RNG) plant.

description:
On June 3, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners authorized staff to apply for the Clean Vessel Act Grant through the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to purchase a septage pumpout boat. The grant was awarded to the County and executed on January 7, 2026, with staff taking delivery of the pumpout vessel on April 13, 2026. The pumpout boat program will operate three days a week, servicing vessels in the Indian River Lagoon outside of marinas with available pumpout.
The Clean Vessel Act was passed in 1992 and provides funding for the construction, operations and maintenance of pumpout equipment and programs. Since 1994, FDEP has awarded nearly $246 million dollars to assist boaters with proper sewage disposal. The Clean Vessel Act Grant Program provides a 75% reimbursement grant for the construction, operation, maintenance, and repair of a pumpout vessel program. Staff is requesting approval to apply for the Clean Vessel Act Grant through two applications, one for the operations and maintenance, and the second for the estimated construction costs of the septage receiving line and associated infrastructure.
title: Clean Vessel Act Grant Applications Request for Operations and Maintenance of the Pumpout Vessel

description: Fish Florida, a non-profit organization whose mission is to promote public awareness of and encourage the protection of marine fisheries and coastal habitats in the State of Florida. Fish Florida provides grants, fishing equipment donations, and scholarships to organizations educating people, especially children, about Florida fish, aquatic habitats and resource stewardship. The Natural Resources Staff are creating an educational outreach and stewardship program that will include fishing clinics for adults and children, and children’s fishing derbies, in support of the Indian River County Indian River Lagoon Management Plan objectives. Fishing derbies provide a unique opportunity to make a lasting impression on the youth of Indian River County by fostering a connection with nature and teaching a life-long skill. The Fish Florida Fishing Equipment Grant will allow staff to supply fishing equipment and materials to participants and successfully run the program.
title: Fish Florida Fishing Equipment Grant

description:
The Hobart Ballfields are part of the larger Kiwanis-Hobart Park Complex, located at the corner of 77th Street and 58th Avenue. In March 1967, the Trust for the Internal Improvement Fund of Florida dedicated 489.61 acres to Indian River County, and in November 1969, an additional 106 acres were acquired from Florida Minerals, further expanding the park complex. Over the years, various grants and donations have supported development of the property, which now includes the Indian River County Fairgrounds, Hobart Ballfields, Kiwanis-Hobart Park, and the Parks Maintenance Office. The park is named in recognition of Mr. Edward Hobart, who contributed $5,000 toward its development, and the Kiwanis Club, which also played a role in developing the park.
The 58th Avenue Ballfield Renovation and Expansion Project began in 2018, with an approved work order issued to Masteller & Moler, Inc. under Work Order No. 5, however, the project experienced several delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic, higher-than-anticipated costs, and a lack of qualified bidders. Bid 2020005 was rejected by the BCC on November 19, 2019 and bid 2024048 was rejected by the BCC on September 24th, 2024.
On behalf of the Parks Division, sealed bids were solicited for construction of the project, which includes the conversion of the existing adult multipurpose field into a college-regulation baseball field; upgrades to an existing softball/little league field; construction of a new softball/hybrid field; lighting improvements; a scoreboard; stormwater improvements; a pump station; parking lot and pathway improvements; landscaping; and construction of a concession/restroom building. The project was designed by Masteller & Moler, Inc., and Bid No. 2025030 was issued on February 9, 2025, with bids received until 2:00 p.m. on March 26, 2025.
title: Change Order for Hobart Ballfield Project

description:
On March 8, 2016, the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) entered into grant Agreement No. S0839 with Indian River County, committing up to $50,000 reimbursement for the construction of an oyster reef project in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL). No local match is required. The grant was initially designated for the construction of an oyster reef at 45th St. Upon closer investigation, the 45th Street site was deemed unsuitable to support the project.
The project was relocated to Foot Island (Lauren's Island), a small area of spoil that was a footing for the previous S.R. 60 bridge. The project became a partnership with the City of Vero Beach. The City provided bathymetric and seagrass surveys, and the County provided the design drawings, permitting, and construction management services.
Initial delays in site selection and permitting required an amendment extending the completion date to December 31, 2024. Permitting was completed, but the initial design and materials exceeded the $50,000.00 threshold by an estimated $250,000.00. Staff identified alternative materials and coordinated with the permitting agencies to modify the permits to reflect the use of the new materials. As a result, staff requested an extension. In response, FDEP issued Amendment No. 4, which extended the agreement date to December 31, 2026.
Installation of the oyster enhancement project was completed in the fall of 2025. To maximize reimbursement, staff requested FDEP revise the agreement to include pre-construction activities.
title: Approval of Amendment No. 5 - FDEP Grant Agreement No. S0839 for Construction of an Oyster Reef at Foot Island in the Indian River Lagoon

description:
The Indian River County Department of Utility Services (IRCDUS) owns and operates the Oslo Water Production Facility (WPF). The existing sand strainer at the facility required replacement to improve system reliability, maintain operational efficiency, and ensure continued delivery of treated water to customers.

The project included procurement and installation of a new sand strainer, associated backwash piping and inlet, stainless steel piping, electrical conduits and wiring, control panel installation, startup, and demolition of the existing sand strainer.
Change Order No. 1 is included as a balancing change order at project closeout to deduct the unused contingency from the contract value. The net decrease associated with Change Order No. 1 is $125,000 with no change to contract time. Thus, the final adjusted contract amount is $782,000.

description:
Floravon Shores is a subdivision of 19 properties on septic systems, adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon (IRL), in North Indian River County. The septic tanks in this area potentially leach harmful nutrients into groundwater that leads to the IRL. The Floravon Shores Septic-to-Sewer (S2S) Project, IRCDUS Project ID 21.19.556, will construct approximately 1,300 linear feet of public gravity sewer infrastructure that consists of new sewer mains and laterals to connect the homes.
It is estimated that the Floravon Shores S2S conversions will result in approximately 950 lbs./year of nitrogen reduction. The S2S conversions will route the wastewater from this community to the County system for collection and treatment at a regional wastewater facility that is operated by Indian River County Department of Utility Services (IRCDUS). The conversions will reduce the nutrient loading, improve water quality, and promote seagrass growth in the IRL.
On April 7, 2026, the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners (BCC) awarded Bid No. 2025045 for the Floravon Shores S2S project to Treasure Coast Infrastructure (TCI) of Stuart in the amount of $896,900 to complete the conversions. No contract documents have been executed to date.

description:
This item requests adoption of a resolution to revise the Indian River County Local Jobs Grant Program and its associated grant agreement.
At its regular meeting in January 2026, the Economic Development Council (EDC) recommended that the County Commission revise the existing Local Jobs Grant Program. The EDC identified three primary goals:
Eliminate unnecessary program complexity
Reduce burdensome compliance requirements
Enhance the return on investment for participating businesses
At the February 2026 Board of County Commissioners meeting, Planning and Development Services staff presented a ten-year performance and utilization analysis of the program and requested authorization to revise it. The analysis showed that the program was underperforming, with only two businesses receiving grant funding during that period.
In addition, past participants and prospective applicants provided feedback to County staff and the Indian River Chamber of Commerce indicating that the program is difficult to understand, overly regulatory, and administratively burdensome. Businesses cited extensive reporting requirements, lengthy agreement terms, and limited financial incentives as barriers to participation and continued compliance. These challenges are particularly significant for small businesses, limiting the program’s effectiveness in supporting job creation.
On February 24, 2026, the Board of County Commissioners authorized staff to revise the program to improve business participation and return with a proposal for future Board consideration.
Following this authorization, County staff initiated revisions based on stakeholder input received from the local business community through County and Chamber outreach. This input guided efforts to address program barriers and improve utilization.
The first step in revising the program was to improve clarity for prospective applicants. Staff developed a set of program guidelines to serve as the primary introductory document. These guidelines outline program components, eligibility criteria, the approval process, project implementation, and reimbursement procedures. The guidelines are included as Exhibit “A” to the Resolution.
The EDC reviewed and approved the guidelines at its March meeting and recommended the following program revisions to be included in the associated agreement:
Reduce the agreement term to a three-year job creation period.
Eliminate multiple hiring phases and commencement dates.
Reduce reporting requirements from quarterly to annual.
Increase the minimum qualifying wage to 100% of the Indian River County average wage.
Increase grant incentives for new jobs and provide additional incentives for jobs paying at least 150% of the County average wage.
Provide full reimbursement after jobs are created and verified through annual reporting.
Include a clawback provision for businesses that do not fulfill commitments made during application and approval.
Planning and Development Services incorporated these recommendations and coordinated with the County Attorney to revise the Local Jobs Grant Program Agreement. The revised agreement is included as Exhibit “B” to the Resolution.
The EDC conducted its final review of the Resolution, guidelines, and agreement at its meeting on May 19, 2026, and unanimously recommended approval by the Board of County Commissioners.
title: Indian River County Local Jobs Grant Program Revision

description: The Indian River County Landfill has a voluntary landfill gas collection system, Landfill Gas Collection and Control System (GCCS), that requires routine and non-routine operations and maintenance (O&M) as well as various expansions. The general purpose of the GCCS is to capture the methane gas to reduce odors, reduce the risk of fires and to reduce it to the less harmful carbon dioxide via flaring in the short run, and to ultimately facilitate the sale of the landfill gas to NoPetro EcoDistrict (NED) for its renewable natural gas (RNG) project. SWDD staff are finalizing a GCCS O&M RFP, which is anticipated to be posted and awarded by July 2026. Since the GCCS has been operational, there is no formal agreement for O&M, which is done at hoc. The majority of work has been done by Integrity Environmental Solutions on a per item basis.
title: Solid Waste Disposal District

description:
The Indian River County (IRC) Solid Waste Disposal District (SWDD) utilizes the Heartland Leachate Evaporator via a long-term agreement with the Indian River Sustainability Center, LLC (IRSC) for onsite treatment of the leachate that is produced from the IRC Class I Landfill. The Leachate Evaporator has a 30,000 gallons per day (GPD) operating capacity and SWDD has a 500,000 gallon leachate storage tank on site. However, SWDD is considering additional leachate pre-treatment capacity for the Class I Landfill, to operate during the rainy season and heavy rain events, with the intention of minimizing the need for off-site treatment at the County's wastewater plant. SWDD's consultant, Geosyntec, requested and evaluated two pilot proposals for the potential long-term use of a reverse osmosis (RO) system.
The proposals were submitted by Sustainable Landfill Solutions (SLS) and IRSC. SLS is a firm specializing in landfill leachate treatment technologies, including modular, scalable systems designed for long-term operational flexibility. IRSC is a provider of industrial water and wastewater treatment solutions, including reverse osmosis and evaporator systems for managing high-strength waste streams. Based on leachate quality, projected volumes, and disposal options, RO was identified as the most viable option to supplement the existing 30,000 GPD gas-fired leachate evaporator based upon a previous evaluation performed by Geosyntec in February 2025. In addition, RO provides effective Per- and Polyfluorinated Substances (PFAS) treatment (if needed) and avoids the cost and permitting challenges associated with adding evaporators or using a deep well injection. The pilot testing will also provide valuable current analytical data for the leachate. Currently, the data is from 2019, and the landfill configuration has changed significantly since then.
title: Request for Approval of Leachate Treatment Pilot Test

description:

title: SWDD Temporary Operation and Maintenance of the IRC Landfill Gas Collection and Control System

description:
Staff is pleased to announce the third year of a generous one-year sponsorship from Route 60 Hyundai totaling $24,000. The Deputy County Administrator, Michael Zito, and the owner of the local businesses, Mr. Chiarenza, met in 2023 to discuss their mutual interest in furthering and expanding the County’s Recreation mission and efforts to provide high quality recreation facilities and programming for the benefit of County residents. Route 60 Hyundai had previously been a sponsor of County Recreation programs before the COVID-19 pandemic. The local dealership is committed to enhancing the lives of Indian River County residents.
The funds will be used toward printing/development of the Fall/Winter Parks and Recreation Brochure, sponsorship of uniforms, recreation supplies and equipment, food for special events and programs, team/league underwriting, and other recreation specific costs that further the mission of the Department.
To recognize the sponsorship, the Parks and Recreation Division will feature Route 60 Hyundai through marketing efforts on marquees, signs/banners, special event t-shirts, digital content, and jerseys of youth basketball, baseball and flag football teams. They will also be featured in the Spring/Summer 2026 Parks and Recreation Brochure. Social media posts will also acknowledge the sponsorship throughout the year.

On January 28, 2025, the Board approved Amendment No. 1, which addressed construction delays and extended the contract time to April 30, 2026. This amendment increased the agreement amount by $237,676.00, resulting in a revised total of $3,236,629.39.

Indian River County Department of Utility Services (IRCDUS) owns and operates the Hobart Water Production Facility (WPF) and Oslo WPF, located at 7751 58th Avenue, Vero Beach and 1550 9th Street SW, Vero Beach, respectively. The water production facilities utilize bulk chemical storage tanks to ensure adequate on-site chemical storage for all treatment needs.
IRCDUS utilizes sodium hypochlorite for disinfection in compliance with state and federal drinking water regulations. Sodium hypochlorite must be stored in approved, properly rated containment tanks that meet current safety and regulatory standards. The Department has identified the need to replace three (3) existing 6,500-gallon sodium hypochlorite bulk storage tanks at the Hobart Water WPF due to structural failure, and to replace one (1) 5,500-gallon Sodium Hypochlorite bulk storage tank at the Oslo Water Production Facility, consistent with the America’s Water Infrastructure Act (AWIA) recommendation to enhance storage capacity resilience.
title: Award of Bid 2025056 for Replacement of (4) Sodium Hypochlorite Storage Tanks

description:
On November 8, 2022, voters approved a referendum allowing for the issuance of up to $50,000,000 of general obligation bonds by the County, payable from ad valorem taxes, to acquire and permanently preserve environmentally significant lands to restore the Indian River Lagoon, protect water resources, natural areas, wildlife habitat, and construct public access improvements.
On January 31, 2023, the Board of County Commissioners (“Board”) approved Resolution 2023-004 which authorized the issuance of general obligation bonds in an aggregate amount not to exceed $50,000,000 to finance the cost of acquisition and construction of public access improvements. The full faith, credit and taxing power of the County is pledged for payment of principal and interest. Resolution 2023-004 provided for the issuance of the bonds in one or more series with further details of the bonds to be approved by supplemental resolutions.
On June 4, 2024, the Board adopted Resolution No. 2024-023 supplementing Resolution No. 2023-004 and authorizing the issuance of General Obligation Bonds, Series 2024 in the exact par amount of $22,795,000. The Series 2024 Bonds were sold at public sale by competitive bid. With the monies issued, the County has begun to acquire environmentally sensitive land and continues to negotiate for the purchase of Tier 1 properties.
To have sufficient funds to continue acquisition efforts, County staff recommends the Board now adopt the attached 2026 Supplemental Resolution to authorize the issuance of General Obligation Bonds, Series 2026 in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $27,205,000. This would be the second and final issue. The Series 2026 Bonds will be sold at public sale by competitive bid. A summary Notice of Sale will be published at least ten (10) days prior to the date of sale. An Official Notice of Sale, Preliminary Official Statement, and A Continuing Disclosure Certificate will be issued in connection with the sale of the Series 2026 Bonds.
Upon approval of the 2026 Supplemental Resolution, the County Administrator and/or the Clerk, or his designee will be authorized and directed to sell the bonds at public sale and award the bonds to the responsive bidder offering to purchase the bonds at the lowest true interest cost to the County, which in no event shall exceed five percent (5.00%), and with a final maturity date no later than twenty (20) years following the date of issuance of the bonds.
title: General Obligation Bonds Series 2026 Supplemental Resolution

description: The Indian River County Correctional Facility’s fire suppression system is failing, and its repair is urgent. The issue was initially identified due to an air leak in the suppression line, which caused the compressor to trip continuously. Due to the current projects underway, the building's interior was open to allow for more detailed inspection. During further inspection and troubleshooting, the piping was found to be brittle, leading to the discovery of significant deterioration within the fire suppression system pipes. If not addressed, the costs to transport and relocate inmates to other facilities could far exceed the costs of the repair.
title: Request for Emergency Repairs to the Correctional Facility Fire Suppression System

description:
The County's six-cent Local Option Gas Tax program was adopted in 1986 with the County sharing the revenue by interlocal agreements with the five municipalities. In 1995, the County Staff met with representatives of all five municipalities to discuss extending the program, and on June 6, 1996, the Local Option Gas Tax agreement was extended for the next 30 years. It terminates on August 31, 2026.
As part of that agreement and as is required by Florida Statute Section 336.025(1)(d) and Chapter 209 of the Indian River County Code, the Board of County Commissioners conducts a public hearing every two years in May to approve a revenue distribution formula for the Local Option Gas Tax. This revenue is shared with the five municipalities based upon the agreement upon formula. The last Public Hearing was on May 21, 2024, therefore a public hearing is required to be held in accordance with the agreement and Indian River County Code this May of 2026.
Additionally, on an annual basis the Local Option Gas Tax Distribution Chart is updated and presented to the Board of County Commissioners and the five municipalities in May to approve a revenue distribution formula for the Local Option Gas Tax. The approved distribution formula is then submitted to the Department of Revenue by the October 1st deadline.
Staff has meet with members of the five municipalities regarding the expiration of the interlocal agreements, and the current method of distribution formula for the local option gas tax. Staff and the municipalities came to agreement on updated interlocal agreements and an updated method of distribution formula for the local option gas tax. Those inter local agreements have been approved by the individual municipalities at a public hearing in front of each respective municipality and are now attached for review and approval by the Board.
title: Local Option Gas Tax Interlocal Agreement/Ordinance Adoption (Legislative)

description: Indian River County entered into a Developer Agreement with the property owner/developer, Novaland, LLC, a Florida limited liability company for property located in the Reams Glen Subdivision on August 20, 2024. This agreement was to allow for the construction and extension of water mains and sewer lines to the properties owned by the owner/developer. The original Developer Agreement called for the owner/developer to obtain easements from the surrounding property owners to place the utility and sewer lines in the private right of way which lies adjacent to the properties being developed. The owner/developer was unable to obtain the easements as the surrounding property owners refused to grant them. The property owner/developer has come back and asked the utilities department let them construct the new utilities/sewer lines in the already existing rear lot utility easements. The utilities department has agreed to allow the use of the rear lot easements. This has caused the need for a reworked water/sewer line plan and an amended Developer Agreement between the County and the owner/developer for the new terms and placement of the utility/sewer lines. Pursuant to Florida Statue Section 163.3225 there are two public hearings required for the approval of any proposed or amended developer's agreement. This hearing shall serve as the second of the two required public hearings. The first required public hearing was held on May 5th at 9:05 am or as soon thereafter.
title: Reams Glen Amended and Reinstated Developer Agreement

description:
At its May 20, 2025 meeting, the Board of County Commissioners (BCC) identified the need for comprehensive planning and regulatory updates tailored to the Oslo Corridor, a high-interest development area currently lacking cohesive land use designations and design standards consistent with the County’s long-term vision.
To support a structured and coordinated planning approach, the BCC adopted an ordinance imposing a one-year temporary moratorium on zoning changes and comprehensive plan land use amendments within the unincorporated portions of Indian River County designated as the Oslo Corridor Study Area.
The one-year temporary moratorium will expire June 17, 2026, and it is requested by staff to extend the temporary moratorium until December 31, 2026, within the unincorporated areas of Indian River County specific to the Oslo Corridor Study Area.
title: Ordinance Authorizing the Extension of a Temporary Moratorium on Zoning Changes and Comprehensive Plan Amendments in the Oslo Corridor Study Area (Legislative)

description:
On June 3, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners BOCC approved the County’s group insurance program for the plan year October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026. During this meeting there was discussion regarding projected plan performance and the potential impact of the increased cost related to GLP-1 for weight loss. It was noted that under the new pharmacy PBM, Rightway, GLP-1 weight loss medications would require prior authorization criteria for BMI and co-morbidity to be met in order to be covered under the plan. Ultimately, there were no changes made to the group health plan, there were no increases in group health plan premiums, and it was determined staff would continue to monitor plan financials and report back to the Board. Since that time, plan experience under our current plan year has reflected a substantial increase in medical claims as well as continued increase in GLP-1 weight loss medications necessitating the Board consider modifications to the plan as well as make necessary premium increases to fund the plan benefits.
Staff met with the Board on March 24, 2026, to discuss group insurance plan performance for the first quarter of our current plan year (FY26 Q1). Staff returned on May 5, 2026 to provide updated financial information through February 2026 as well as March 2026 financial highlights and to provide recommendations for plan modifications, funding requirements and premium amounts for the upcoming plan year.
Staff will meet with the Board on May 19, 2026, to receive direction on plan modifications, funding and premium amounts for the plan year beginning October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027.
Once the Board provides direction regarding the Employee and Employer contribution rates, staff recommends directing Lockton to rebalance the Employer contribution so that the County maintains equal contributions towards family and single coverage, regardless of Silver or Gold plan as well as reflect the 25% increase in the employee contribution for both family and single coverage under each plan. The impact of this rebalancing is projected to be minimal. The rebalancing would include the staff recommendation to increase premiums by 25% of the current monthly rates. These premium amounts will be generated by Lockton consistent with funding requirements and will be reviewed with the Board at the May 19th meeting.
title: Group Health Insurance Recommendations for Plan Year FY26/27

description:
On December 3, 1984, the Board of County Commissioners adopted Ordinance 1984-081, which established the Vero Lakes Estate MSTU Advisory Committee (VLEMSTUAC). The committee has been dormant. The Vero Lake Estates Property Owners Association (POA) contacted Commissioner Susan Adams regarding its desire to restart the committee. Public Works staff and the County Attorney’s office met with the Vero Lake Estates POA to discuss restarting the committee. The County Attorney prepared the committee’s vacancy notice and published it on the County’s Website and social media platform. It is also posted on the Vero Lake Estates Property Owners Association website.

description:
The Florida Development Finance Corporation (“FDFC”), created per Chapter 288, Part X, Florida Statutes issues bonds to finance and refinance projects for the benefit of Florida businesses to enhance the economic development of the State of Florida. On November 5, 2013, the FDFC and the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners (“Board”) entered into an Interlocal Agreement, which permits the FDFC to issue bonds to finance and refinance projects within Indian River County, subject to the Board’s reserved right to consent to each such project. Coastal Waste and Recycling Inc. has requested the issuance of FDFC Revenue Bonds in the amount of up to $250,000,000 to finance or refinance improvements to solid waste facilities. According to a FDFC representative, the primary purpose of the bond money that will be spent in Indian River County will be for Coastal Waste & Recycling to develop a construction and demolition debris (C&D) material recovery facility (MRF) in Vero Beach, Florida across from the County's landfill ("Project"). FDFC has provided this additional information about the Project:
Indian River County Hauling & Recycling Project
The C&D MRF is designed to process debris generated from construction, renovation, and demolition activities, including concrete, asphalt, wood, metals, drywall, and plastics. By implementing advanced sorting technologies and recovery systems, the facility aims to maximize material diversion from landfills, support circular economy principles, and meet growing regulatory and sustainability demands in Indian River County and the surrounding municipalities. The C&D MRF will process approximately 1,440 tons per day, resulting in more than 220,000 tons being diverted from landfills on an annual basis. Approximately $2M of the proceeds of the Series 2026 Bonds will be used to fund equipment purchases along with related development and construction costs associated with the site and structures. The Indian River County Hauling & Recycling facility is poised to deliver substantial economic and environmental benefits to the community. By increasing recycling capacity, lowering costs, and supporting local sustainability initiatives, the facility will help drive progress toward a circular economy, reduce landfill dependency, and create new opportunities for growth and environmental stewardship.
FDFC is seeking the consent of the Board for the issuance of bonds for this Project. Indian River County shall have no responsibility with respect to the repayment of the bonds, and the bonds will not constitute an indebtedness or pledge of the general credit or taxing power of the County.
title: Florida Development Finance Corporation Consent Resolution For Coastal Waste and Recycling, Inc.

It is common throughout the County to use canal rights-of-way for County roads. Most of the canal rights-of-way are 100 feet in width, so there is room for a canal and a road within that 100 feet. Historically, the roads along side the canals were used to maintain the canal, but as the County grew in population, those roads were improved to accommodate the increase in traffic. An example of this would be 74th Avenue. The canal is on the east side of 74th Avenue and the road itself is adjacent to the canal to the west, within the canal right-of-way. But along 74th Avenue between 1st Street SW and 5th Street SW, private property lies to the west of the canal, then there is a 20-foot gap, and then there is a 30-foot wide strip of right-of-way. There is no roadway in the 30-foot right-of-way strip, as the roadway lies next to the canal in the seemingly privately owned property. Please see the attached sketch as a sample of the situation along this stretch of 74th Avenue. The County maintains 74th Avenue between 1st Street SW and 5th Street SW as a two lane, paved, public roadway.
While this situation has existed since 1956, it now needs to be resolved. Florida Public Utilities, formerly known as Florida City Gas, needs to install a gas line along 74th Avenue to supply natural gas to the improvements being constructed at the County Landfill. As it stands now, there is insufficient room to install the line without correcting the right-of-way configuration. In order to rectify this error, the County proposes an even exchange of land without consideration with the affected property owners along 74th Avenue. The effected property owners are Pellegrino and Michelle Barone (Barone), Oslo Road Agriculture, LLC (Oslo) and Beale Holdings, Inc. (Beale). The County has prepared the attached Property Exchange Agreement and approving Resolution in order for the parcels to be exchanged. Oslo has returned their signed Agreement, but the other owners have not. The other two parties have verbally agreed to the Agreement. The Parties will exchange Quit Claim Deeds as provided in the Agreement for equal amounts of property and the County will record the deeds with the corrected legal descriptions.
Pursuant to Florida Statutes §125.37 the proposed exchange was published in the local newspaper once a week for at least two weeks before the Board can adopt the Resolution authorizing the exchange. Advertising was published on April 21 2026, and April 28, 2026.
title: 74th Avenue Property Exchange with Pellegrino and Michelle Barone, Oslo Road Agriculture, LLC and Beale Holdings, Inc.

description:
The subject properties, comprising approximately ±7.79 acres, are located on the north side of 45th Street, approximately 0.45 miles east of 58th Avenue. The properties are zoned RS-6, Single-Family Residential District, and RMH-8, Residential Mobile Home District, (see Attachment 1). They are within the Urban Service Area (USA), and have a Future Land Use designation of M-2, Medium-Density Residential-2 (up to 10 units/acre) (see Attachment 2). The applicant’s justification letter states, “A rezoning of approximately 7.79 acres, from Residential Single-family (RS-6) and Residential Mobile Home (RMH-8) to Multiple-family Residential (RM-6) to allow a combination of single family, and shared wall villas (in duplex or triplex groupings). The objective is to eliminate the two-zoning classifications and create an RM- 6 zoned district to establish a residential community mixing single family and shared wall villas that are affordable to further Habitat for Humanity’s goal and vision. This property is uniquely situated to utilize RM-6 as a zoning transition area between the mobile home communities to the west and the single-family homes to the east. Also, on 45th Street, the properties to the south are a mix of industrial zoning and Commercial/Industrial land uses. The 45th Street corridor is an important part of the Gifford community, which offers community services like the Gifford Health Center and Gifford Youth Center. 45th Street is serviced by Route 14 of the Go Line, a free bus service. Route 14 connects to Route 9, as well as Route 8 and Route 3 to provide transportation to many parts of the County.”
The requested RM-6 zoning is compatible with the M-2 Future Land Use designation while maintaining compatible residential densities with surrounding RS-6 and RMH-8 districts. The proposed rezoning does not increase the allowable density but instead facilitates a broader range of attainable housing types to support affordable housing objectives. As such, the request reflects a zoning consolidation that preserves the area’s established residential character while enabling a context-sensitive mix of units aligned with community needs.
The Comprehensive Plan specifies under Single-Family (Page 15) that “Overall, commercial and industrial uses in the Gifford area are located along the US 1/Old Dixie Highway corridor and on the two major east/west roads, 41st Street and 45th Street. As referenced in the Housing Element, this area has a large number of incompatible land uses with inadequate buffering between them. The Housing Element also identifies Gifford as an area that contains a large number of persons below the poverty level and living in substandard housing.”
The Comprehensive Plan also specifies under The Residential Designations, Medium Density (Page 180) that “Medium density areas are located along major transportation routes near shopping, employment, and service centers. Located along US 1, along Indian River Blvd., along SR 60, and in Gifford, these land use designations are intended for multiple-family apartments, condominiums, townhouses, and mobile home developments.”
Existing Land Use Pattern
The surrounding area reflects a residential development pattern along the north side of 45th Street that is characterized primarily by single-family residential subdivisions and Mobile Homes. Adjacent to the west of the site along 45th Street are multiple parcels zoned RMH-8, developed with mobile homes in the 1980s. To the northwest lies the Shannon Walks Subdivision, zoned RS-6 and platted in 2000. Directly north is the Lindsey Lanes Subdivision, also zoned RS-6 and platted in 2001. Further northeast is the Gifford Community and Aquatic Center. Adjacent to the east is Cavalier Estates, a historic RS-6-zoned subdivision platted in 1957. Further east along 45th Street and south across from the site is the Gifford Node, identified in Table 2.5 of the 2006 Commercial/Industrial Nodes. This area also includes the West Gifford Industrial and Commerce Overlay (Section 911.23 of the Indian River County Land Development Regulations) and is primarily zoned General Industrial (IG).
Collectively, the surrounding development pattern along 45th Street reflects a diverse but increasingly residential character, transitioning from older mobile home developments and historic subdivisions to more modern single-family neighborhoods. The subject properties’ M-2, Medium-Density Residential-2 Future Land Use designation aligns with this evolving character. The requested rezoning from RS-6 and RMH-8, to RM-6 ,would consolidate zoning on the site and establish a compatible residential transition between adjacent mobile home communities and single-family neighborhoods. Located along 45th Street, a key east-west corridor serving the Gifford area, the site is also situated near an established industrial node to the south. The proposed zoning supports a balanced land use pattern and reinforces the corridor’s function as both a residential and service-oriented spine, consistent with the Comprehensive Plan.
Zoning District Differences
In terms of permitted uses, there are both similarities and differences between the existing RMH-8 & RS-6 district and the proposed RM-6 district (See Attachment 3 for a zoning district comparison table). The distinctions between these three zoning districts are best illustrated through their respective purpose statements, as outlined in the County’s Land Development Regulations (LDRs). These purpose statements provide a clear framework for understanding the intent and scope of each district's allowable uses and development potential. The purpose statements are as follows:
RHM-8: Residential Mobile Home District (up to 8 units/acre): This district is intended to provide areas suitable for medium-density mobile home residential development, up to 8 units per acre. The RMH-8, Residential Mobile Home District is established to implement the Comprehensive Plan’s residential land use policies, support a diverse housing supply through mobile home opportunities, and ensure adequate public facilities to meet the needs of residents.
RS-6: Single-Family Residential District (up to 6 units/acre): This district is intended to provide areas suitable for moderate-density single-family residential development, up to 6 units per acre. The RS-6, Single-Family Residential District is intended to implement the Comprehensive Plan policies for residential areas, support single-family housing opportunities, and ensure the provision of adequate public facilities to serve residents.
RM-6: Multiple-Family Residential District (up to 6 units/acre): This district is intended to provide areas suitable for medium-density multiple-family residential development, as well as single-family dwellings, up to 6 units per acre. The RM-6, Multiple-Family Residential District is intended to ensure adequate public facilities to meet the needs of residents, as well as provide a varied and diverse housing supply.
title: Indian River County Habitat for Humanity, Inc.'s Request to Rezone Approximately 7.79 Acres [Quasi-Judicial]
